Um. 4 blood = 4 blood, therefore the acting vampire. 4 pool would be
4 pool. And the symbol on the card has a great big "4" on it in the
"blood off a vampire" spot. This is the same format all the other
cards are in...?

>Why exactly is this card supposed to be broken and how is this
>supposed to fix it? The fix just seems to be an invitation for some
>other player to come across table and take out the acting vampire
>before the effect finally kicks in. This seems an ugly and unreliable
>fix - just like the fix to Wake.

It is, in fact, such an invitation.

The original version of the card was:

Cost: 4 blood
Requires a ready vampire.
(D) Bleed your prey with +X bleed, where X is the capacity of the
acting vampire. Burn this vampire if this action is successful.

So you got out Arika, Minion Tapped her down to 6, and bled with this
card. Day Op for unblockable, and Conditioning for a bleed modifier
afterwards; total bleed amount = 3 + 11 + 3 = 17. This was usually
enough to oust almost anyone, and resulted in everyone being forced to
pack 12 Deflections in their deck, or risk being ousted at any given
time - since even if you weren't the original target of the bleed, it
was likely to get bounced to you. Archon Investigation was
insufficient, as you needed it on the -top- of your deck.

"Hideously Broken" wasn't an accurate description. AND you could do
it with any big vampire, due to the discipline-lessness of the card.
AND, because of the ill-worded "Burn" on the card, you could perform
elaborate Soul Gem tricks.

Several different errata were tried, and none really proved useful, as
you had to be playing combat *and* get through an Obedience wall in
order to actually remove blood from the vampire in question and negate
the card. The NJL tried "no action modifiers may be played with this
card", so you couldn't Day Op or add stealth to it, but this left the
door open for the Concoction of Vitality and Marked Path.

In the end, it was decided that having the ability to bleed for 10 or
more with one card was unbalancing, and the card was banned... thank
god.

Messages.Author: Ian Lee
Messages.Body:
>the big mistake that magic always made, and which v:tes has
>certainly also made, is in how they react to overpowered or unbalancing
>cards. ban them, change their text ridiculously, or change the actual
>rules as a reaction to their use. WRONG! this is flat-out WRONG
>thinking, to my mind.

My experience has been that some cards are so bad that trying to work around
them produces long term flaws in the game.

What happens too often, when hoser cards are made, is that the game becomes
unstable. The broken strategy is still broken as long as the counter isn't
played. If it is, the broken strategy often becomes completely ineffectual.

Personally, I find the volume of errata in this game to be a joke. I'm amazed
people find the game playable, yet we find a way. The negative effects of
errata can be somewhat mitigated with reprinting cards with correct text, which
sometimes happens and sometimes doesn't.

As for banning, I've learned to be heavily in favor of banning. It's so much
easier to remember a list of cards than to remember how card texts have
changed. But, most CCG companies never want to ban anything because then they
will look like WotC. Also, for some reason, players scream bloody murder about
how they can't play their cards. Apparently, CCGs attract numerous power
gamers. There's also a limit to how many cards can be banned. Archon
Investigation, for instance, seems to be an attempt to fix a group of
strategies not one card. Banning Conditioning, Govern, etc. doesn't seem
realistic.

There will always be problem cards. Having playtested quite a bit for a few
games, I don't see how playtesting will ever catch every problem. What to do
with the problems has no simple solution, for if it did, everyone would use it.
And, not every problem should be looked in the same way. Sometimes trying to
work around a problem card/strategy is the best solution. Sometimes a
different response is best.

I have zero problem with Return being banned. I played in a tournament game
where every player was ousted with it (original text). It was just too
disruptive.

As a last comment, no doubt brought up often when discussing the problems with
big bleed that produced Archon Investigation in the first place, players adapt.
However, the metagame should be open to as many different strategies as
possible. If adapting means playing proX or counterX only, the game isn't
likely to be much fun. Adapting can solve many problems but not all.

I question whether printing "power" vampires adds anything to the
game, other than fierce contesting of the "power" vampires. Jimmy
Dunn functions well partly because of his special disability re:
contesting, and partly because he is highly specialized. If you're
not beating things up, you don't have Jimmy. And if you do use Jimmy,
you have to be wary of someone else wanting that same Jimmy.

>methuselahs could bestow these devastating capabilities on their
>minions.

and I also question whether providing "devastating capabilities" is
such a good idea. The game balance would have to be carefully taken
into consideration, especially when introducing a discipline via
Master cards only. As a "master-only" discipline, the inferior of
most cards would have to be highly effective, and the superior even
MORE so, to reward the problems encountered in getting the discipline
onto vampires in the first place. So now you have to carefully
balance every single card printed to avoid accidentally providing too
much support to one discipline or another; and there are an awful lot
of disciplines and combos out there already.

It becomes somewhat like equipment, actually. There is an awful lot
of good equipment out there. But you don't see it used much, because
it's difficult to get into play and difficult to keep in play, and
easy to get hosed. So even though the relative power-per-cost of
equipment has increased substantially (compare Bang Nakh, Crimson
Sentinel, and Femur of Toomler to the original Jyhad toys), you still
don't hear about anyone's fabulous Bang Nakh deck because it's STILL
almost not worth the time to equip it. Is the solution to keep
increasing the power of equipment? No, since then you get into an
"arms race" where eventually you have something that's just TOO good,
and tips over the balance. Same with the new disciplines. Making
them weak will just make them ignored. Making them good is difficult
without accidentally making them TOO good.

>although there are a ton of overpowered cards on lasombra's site, WW
>should check out some of the card ideas linked there. i favor a full
>run of the following (viable) clans: !assem, !ravnos, SoL, and

I favor getting Final Nights out first to fix the Independent clans
(Ravnos/Giovanni/Setite/Assamite), and then doing a partial reprint of
the base set to give new players a solid platform to start from that
they can combine with the reprint of Sabbat War. A new player can do
OK with Sabbat War right now, but the "original seven" clans need to
be available in stores as well.

First, only something like seven cards have been banned. A pretty
good track record, since most of them have OBVIOUS problems in
tournament play.

Some cards are sufficiently broken that immediate repair is required.
(see: RtI) This is V:TES, not Magic. We don't get expansions every
two months - for the past two years, we weren't even sure we would GET
another expansion. Banning or errata wasn't just an unpleasant
option, it was the ONLY option.

How do you deal with Madness of the Bard, for example? Aside from the
problems it causes for non-native-language speakers, it relies on a
totally subjective interpretation of what a "rhyme" is. No two people
are likely to agree. One person on here believes that simply
repeating the sentence twice qualifies as a rhyme; I would NEVER
permit such a thing as a judge, but that just points up the real
problem with the card, that it's totally dependent on who's judging.

So you have to ban the card. There's no other way.

>these expansions, print cards, possibly even common cards, that take

>card. example: there is a problem with return to innocence. instead of
>changing the card text to something unrecognizable as the card text, use
>one of your reprint slots to reprint Archon Investigation, and also make

Besides that Archon Investigation is not an adequate solution to
RtI... see below for why trying to "fix" broken cards with other cards
is a bad idea.

>a new reaction card like SEEN FROM A MILE AWAY:reaction,common,costs 1
>from the vamp;if an opponent is bleeding you for more than 3 pool, tap
>this minion--this bleed is reduced to 1 and no further modifiers may be
>played on this bleed. it's simple, it's not unbalanced... do you

Actually, it's dreadfully unbalanced, since it drastically weakens
bleed as a strategy. Bleeding is already balanced out sufficiently by
intercept and Deflection; it doesn't need to have a magic card
available to everyone that negates one of its strengths,... that it
can do more than 3 at a time. If I can only do 3 pool loss max, why
not just play a vote deck? Much easier, comes with +1 stealth on all
actions by default...

>really risk the loss of that inner circle member if dimple might see
>that return to innocence coming from a mile away??? maybe you do, and
>that re-vitalizes not only return to innocence, but cards that let you
>peek at your prey's hand...

Return to Innocence does not need to be revitalized. It needs to be
gone, and stay gone. The game was not designed to handle bleeds of
10-15 from a single vampire in one action.

I mentioned above the other problem with fixing cards by printing
other cards. You turn it into an "arms race", where you're either
playing the RtI deck, or you're playing with a copy of this new
reaction, or you're being ousted. It also sharply reduces the deck
variety possible; for example, where is the room for combat in this?
Most combat decks couldn't afford the 8 Wakes and 8 copies of your
reaction that would be REQUIRED to provide a defense against RtI.

It's been generally agreed here that any situation where you are
forced to either play "X" or play "anti-X" is a Bad Thing, and
something for the game as a whole to avoid moving towards. To that
extent, the suitable approach to fixing broken cards is to fix the
card, NOT to layer band-aids on top of it.

>also, ON REPRINTS: someone suggested that complaining about reprints is

They aren't ultra-common unless you have purchased a lot of the
original Jyhad base set. In the current set (and only one White Wolf
has been responsible for, FYI), Sabbat War, The Barrens is only found
in the preconstructed Brujah and Lasombra decks. This makes it easily
available for people who want one, and also no longer "common".

New players may not want the original Jyhad set, because the card
backs do not match. They may not want to go chasing after the old
"Vampire" starter set, which is old, slightly more expensive, and
currently filled with incorrect card text. This is why the Barrens
was reprinted in Sabbat War; because the usefulness of the card is
undeniable, and it needs to be available in a suitable fashion. As
much as we'd all love to see 437 new cards, it's not appropriate for
new players, which is something this game desperately needs.

I believe that ideas are fine, but the objection that Wizards raised
(and I suspect White Wolf echoes) is against specific card texts. So
it'd be OK to hold a discussion on, say, a hypothetical Auspex card
that got around S:CE somehow, and which clans it would benefit, and
why it should be in Auspex instead, and should it be only superior,
etc... but spewing out card text just makes things difficult for WW.

the problem lies in the recent American tendency towards frivolous
lawsuits. Fighting those costs money, time, and effort, and could
well delay an entire expansion over one card that someone with more
money than sense believed was "his intellectual property", and that
somehow "he came up with it first". So ideas are great, but please...
no specific card texts, no specific card titles.

>nobody commented on my opinions of which clans/new disciplines/and how

Well... I'm still formulating a concrete opinion on new clans,
disciplines, etc. There's been such a froth over it recently, with
one person claiming that any new disciplines are a Horrible Bad Idea
and that it would Just Ruin the game, and quite a lot of
counterargument, and then a couple others leaping in in support of the
other side... that I'm taking my time before wading into that one, to
be sure I have solid examples.

I can summarise my position thusly: I believe that adding new clans
and disciplines to the game is the ONLY WAY to guarantee a
consistently growing player base, because you MUST have a marketing
tie-in. Some people love the Gangrel, true, and adding the occasional
new toy for the Gangrel is great... but the Gangrel are quite viable
the way they are, and there's no need to screw with that. Taking a
brand-new clan and simply making them a subset of a previous clan and
a previous discipline just won't thrill people. The average person
wants New n' Shiny, and a New Clan with New Toys is it.

I also believe that adding new clans and disciplines, if/when it's
done, must be done properly, so that we don't end up with the problems
that the Ravnos, Giovanni, Assamites, and Setites had for so long.
The two major weak points in the DS/AH expansions were:

1) Not enough vampires, or vampires that sucked
2) Not enough discipline cards that didn't suck

Both of these can be laid directly at the door of the design team and
playtesters, who should have KNOWN better than to let this sort of
thing out the door. Exception must be made for whoever designed the
Ravnos vampires, though, because damn near all of them are quite
effective and focused; now the LIBRARY cards, those could use help.

#1 can be easily fixed. Print 12 vampires per new clan. Each of them
should have either inferior or superior of the new discipline. Enough
of the larger vampires should have the superior that it is possible to
make a deck "go" without use of skill cards. Make sure that you keep
the disciplines relatively focused on the in-clans - don't create
vampires like Aisha (ani aus PRE ser), who have disciplines scattered
all to hell and gone and a convenient special to try to make up for
it. She should've been (obf PRE SER) and the same special, and THEN
she would've been functional.

#2 can be easily fixed as well; if a card requires conditions that are
excruciatingly rare, then DON'T PRINT IT unless the benefits of the
card are huge. Simple playtesting would have solved a lot of the
problems; I have no idea what the writer of Death Pact was thinking,
with the multiple ultra-rare conditions layered on top of each other.

The "fragmentation" issue is one I'd like to save for later, since I
have some pretty firm ideas but need to work up a solid basis to
present them on.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 12 Nov 2000 spin...@my-deja.com wrote:
> the person with the idea that certain disciplines, nay possibly whole
> (small) clans could be represented by card texts is on the right track.
> if you only print one Salubri, and one True Brujah, and one baali, then
> they just get used as SUPPLEMENTS to the existing jyhad of the
> methuselahs. you don't have to print 12 vamps of varying ages and
> skills that make say, Salubri, viable. if the Salubri's healing
> capability proves nasty enough in combo with their skills, they will be
> a vamp that a methuselah covets control of, like certain other vamps
> have always been (rake, agrippina, black cat, violette prentiss...)
> where Mortis needs to be different than necromancy, just use special
> card text. the same with obeah/van. give a couple Salubri/samedi
> special skills in their card text.

The problems with doing this are that you then limit your options for the
future.

Assume that Wizards of the Coast had decided with Sabbat that, well, Jyhad
wasn't really viable and they'd make this their last expansion, and they
would bother after that. So, they printed a Salubri with text as you
suggest.

Now, several years down the line, we have White Wolf in control. Several
years ago, we couldn't have predicted that at all. With changes that
occur in the World of Darkness, printing just a couple of vampires with
special abilities means that you end up cutting off future
possibilities. How do you then, later, integrate that clan in when you
want to do them as a whole clan?

> oddly, i think that the 2
> Disciplines that need to be disciplines and have specialized cards
> printed for them are Temporis and Daimoinon.

Daimoinon is a possibility, of course, but many, many people have
objections to Temporis, in my experience. As a discipline in V:tM, it was
the very epitomy of stupidity. Time-travel and such like always ends up
screwing with games for people. I think it was Xian, or someone, who
mentioned recently when this topic came up, how many times have we all
heard players saying "Hey, we'll go back in time and kill...."

Bang goes your story arc. Maybe we could go back in time and convince
people that the Salubri are actually a bunch of cuddly people after all,
and the Tremere shouldn't ever do nasty things to them. And....

> one more philosophical thing. this is to the WHITE WOLF REP and
> everyone. the big mistake that magic always made, and which v:tes has
> certainly also made, is in how they react to overpowered or unbalancing
> cards. ban them, change their text ridiculously, or change the actual
> rules as a reaction to their use. WRONG! this is flat-out WRONG
> thinking, to my mind.

Many differing approaches were looked at when such problems were brought
up.

There were many different thoughts. Some people like the shock nature of
such power cards, others preferred small errata, others major errata,
others banning. Everything comes down to a judgement call in the end, but
all the options were thoroughly discussed at the time.

> accept that you will be printing expansions. in
> these expansions, print cards, possibly even common cards, that take
> care of the problem or add another facet to the metagame of using that
> card.

Well, there are many problems with this.

1) You assume you are going to get an expansion. When the problems with
Return to Innocence were encountered and addressed by LSJ, the chances of
V:TES *ever* getting an expansion were slim. Very slim.

2) What happens before you get the expansion. Okay, cool. We don't
errata X because we can address it later. Well, for six months now we
still have to carry on playing with a completely broken card. If there is
a problem with a card, it does need to be addressed. Waiting six months,
a year or more for a new expansion to come out takes a lot of time.

3) The cash-cow mentality. If you, to compete with Return to Innocence,
need a card in Final Nights, it produces a situation where people pretty
much have to buy Final Nights or die (to take random situations
here). So, people have to buy Final Nights. People can end up resenting
doing that. As it currently stands, people with a reasonably large card
pool taken at random have an excellently workable situation to work
with. About 500-600 cards works well (the size of a box of Jyhad
boosters).

Take, for example, the card Corruption in Ancient Hearts. It uses old,
established mechanisms and can be countered via old, established
mechanisms. You don't *have* to buy Ancient Hearts, you can play with
your Jyhad/V:TES set and still find all the cards you need to deal with
it. Sure, you can add cards from elsewhere, but you don't *need*
to.

Creating situations where you *need* to buy new cards creates unrest. Not
everyone can afford to buy new cards all the time, some of us have other
commitments. And good will of players counts for a whole lot.

> example: there is a problem with return to innocence. instead of
> changing the card text to something unrecognizable as the card text, use
> one of your reprint slots to reprint Archon Investigation, and also make
> a new reaction card like SEEN FROM A MILE AWAY:reaction,common,costs 1
> from the vamp;if an opponent is bleeding you for more than 3 pool, tap
> this minion--this bleed is reduced to 1 and no further modifiers may be
> played on this bleed. it's simple, it's not unbalanced...

Okay, first of all, you need to be reacting. Not all decks are designed
to do a lot of reacting.

Second of all, is it not unbalanced? Well, it might or might not be. But
look at it this way:

If I create a piece of errata for a card, I can target that
*specific* card. Same applies to banning it. If I create other
cards, it's much more difficult.

What does your card actually do? Well, it kills Return to
Innocence. Definitely. No arguments there. But it doesn't *just* kill
Return to Innocence. It really hurts stealth-bleed decks, which are in a
situation where they're pretty much balanced at the moment. They
certainly aren't, in my experience, winning a completely unbalancing
number of tournaments. Then there's your bruise and bleed. When bruise
and bleed does find a gap to get through, it needs to be able to bleed for
a fair bit - and your card stacks against that, too. (This is one of the
commoner complaints against Protected Resources (also known as Protected
Racehorses, if Deja ever puts it archive back on-line).)

See, when you target bleed, you don't just target Return to
Innocence. You change the whole face of the game.

If the problem is *only* with Return to Innocence, just affecting that one
card can be a way, way simpler method of achieving a balanced environment
whilst simultaneously not completely resculpting that environment under
everyone's feet.

> also, ON REPRINTS: someone suggested that complaining about reprints is
> wrong because there is always some use to 40 copies of a card...

With a number of cards, there can be.

> i
> offer them as many THE BARRENS as they can handle.

Sure, but what do you do with new players who don't have the cards?

> truly wallpaper.

Not at all.

There are a number of common thoughts in the game about some things, a
number of which are just plain wrong. One of the things that sets Jyhad
apart from Magic is the replacement mechanism.

If I play Magic, I always replenish cards, regardless. I can speed that
up, sure, but I can be pretty much sure of getting a card every turn,
without doing *anything*. Jyhad works with a constant replace mechanism,
instead. If you don't get rid of cards, you can't get new ones. The
Barrens is an excellent way of providing extra card cycling. If I get
into sticky situations, I can speed up the rate at which I sift through my
deck. I can try and pull out new cards which will help me, sifting out
the cards that are screwing me up at the moment.

Sure, you're never going to want 40 in a deck, but that's a problem with
any card game where you only have two or three different rarities -
common, uncommon and rare. Some of the commons you want a lot of, some of
them you don't. It happens.

> reprinters at white wolf should look at the usefulness of each card if
> you have 2, 10, and 50. yeah, i can make a case for 50 theft of vitae,
> or blood dolls in my collection. but the barrens?

50, no, I can't see any use for that many (other than multiple decks, for
demos and such-like).

But how do you propose to provide the cards to brand new players without
repriting them?

> elder library? deer
> rifle? surely these are cards nobody really wants more than 10 of.

There's a case for lots of copies of deer rifle. The weenie Brujah decks
that sometimes get rolled out find it to be excellent combat
defence. Having to draw *2* maneuvers to stay at close range against a
deck is a fairly stiff problem.

Would everyone want them? Unlikely. But some people do.

> if
> white wolf can not come up with balanced useful alternatives to these
> ULTRACOMMONS,

They're not really ultra-common, they're just common.

And if the point is that you wouldn't want more than, say, 10 discard
locations, creating an alternative doesn't really help. If you don't want
more than 10 Barrens, why do you want 10 Barrens and 10 Barrens Mark 2?

> there
> are endless possibilities that haven't been touched for every discipline
> and clan,

true, there are endless possibilities. But a lot of them should remain
endless.

One of my arguments against the idea of creating meta-disciplines, the
sort favoured by the players who don't want to see Thanatosis brought into
the game in favour of new cards for Necromancy which do the same, is that
I don't like the idea of making every discipline end up doing
everything. Each discipline is unique and does its own
thing. Cross-over, sure, but Necromancy shouldn't be the premier bleed
discipline, nor should Obfuscate be the offensive combat discipline or
whatever. Staying away from such things is Good.

> as well as new allies, equipment and retainers, vote
> modifiers, referendum ideas, actions, locations, combat cards, and

True. But that doesn't stop you, at the same time, providing old staples
so that everyone can play sealed deck right out of the starter and
booster. If you just create infinite subtle variations, so that you don't
re-print old cards, what's the point? You can't use all of them in a
deck, so why not just re-print the old card?

And in situations where you could have both the original and the variation
in a deck, and want that, you provide a real benefit to old players. They
have both, so they can compete better. The newbie can't, since they can't
get access to the old card and so get trashed at the tournament and decide
to give up the game. (This really does happen.)

If you just reprint the old version, no-one gets an advantage in terms of
card availability.

Misdirection (which now only taps a single minion, rather than X minions), to
the point that I don't think weenie bleed is any longer any more effective than
any other good strategy.

Messages.Author: Nystulc
Messages.Body:
In article <7hmt0tcapf0bo5c4p...@4ax.com>, Derek Ray
<lor...@yahoo.com> writes:

>Well... I'm still formulating a concrete opinion on new clans,
>disciplines, etc. There's been such a froth over it recently, with
>one person claiming that any new disciplines are a Horrible Bad Idea
>and that it would Just Ruin the game,

I can only presume this is intended to be a paraphrase of my views. As such,
it requires some clarification. My opinion expressed was that new disciplines
would, *if* incorporated in the traditional V:tES manner damage the
marketability of the game by fragmenting the customer base, and making it
harder to satisfy the entire available customer base with each expansion. I
therefore advocated that new disciplines not be incorporated in the traditional
manner, with their own crypt-card symbol and a host of support crypt and
library cards to support them. Instead I advocated that new concepts be
incorporated in such a manner that they interact easily within the existing
structure.

I never claimed that new disciplines would "just ruin the game" in the sense of
making it unplayable or less fun (which I believe is what the phrase implies).
My concerns, very specifically expressed, addressed its marketabilty and
profitability. Considering that Wizards of the Coast gave up on the game,
there was already reason to suspect that the game's profitability was hovering
somewhere on the borders of survival. If the game ceases to be profitable,
then it will not be marketted or promoted, and, in the long run, is likely to
be less played. If the player base is fragmented, it becomes, for all
practical purposes, smaller.

>and quite a lot of
>counterargument, and then a couple others leaping in in support of the
>other side... that I'm taking my time before wading into that one, to
>be sure I have solid examples.
>
>I can summarise my position thusly: I believe that adding new clans
>and disciplines to the game is the ONLY WAY to guarantee a
>consistently growing player base, because you MUST have a marketing
>tie-in.

This seems a very extreme position to take. I am confused as how adding new
clans and disciplines will assist in enhancing the player base, much less
GUARANTEE such, much less be the ONLY such strategy worthy of consideration. I
could be wrong, but I just cannot see how a V:tM player player will be
convinced to try V:tES because of a new expansion introduces the new discipline
of Spiritus, when they could not be lured by its featuring of Animalism,
Auspex, Celerity, Chimeristry, Dementate, Dominate, Fortitude, Necromancy,
Obfuscate, Obtenebrate, Potence, Presence, Protean, Quietus, Serpentis,
Thaumaturgy, or Vicissitude. Indeed, it seems more likely that the sheer
number of clans and disciplines will intimidate new players (one of the reasons
I favor focussed expansions).

Indeed, my concern was that any marginal gains in the player base made by such
a strategy (if any) would be more than offset by the "fragmentation" of the
interests of the existing customer base, such it would be more difficult to
keep all players interested in every expansion. While the overall number of
V:tES players MIGHT rise, a smaller percentage of these would be interested in
each expansion, since its cards would be less likely to interact with those
they prefer to play. For all practical purposes, fragmentation reduces the
player base for each expansion.

I do of course agree that new expansions are essential for marketing the game
and keeping alive. I do not see why new disciplines MUST necessarily be part
of this strategy.

Of course, I am not against adding new things. Rather I am against adding new
things in an unnecessarily fragmenting manner. Will introducing the "Mortis"
the "new discipline" really have greater marketing value than introducing
"Mortuus" the new set of powers for an old discipline? Thematically, they are
virtually identical, so if one can be used for marketing, so can the other.

>Some people love the Gangrel, true, and adding the occasional
>new toy for the Gangrel is great... but the Gangrel are quite viable
>the way they are, and there's no need to screw with that. Taking a
>brand-new clan and simply making them a subset of a previous clan and
>a previous discipline just won't thrill people. The average person
>wants New n' Shiny, and a New Clan with New Toys is it.

I presume you are talking about veteran players here, who have already
collected all the "old Toys". It seems to me difficult to believe that any
player fanatic enough to have collected cards from all 22 clans and all 17
disciplines, in numbers sufficient to be playable, will somehow lose interest
and stop playing just because he does not get a 23rd and a 18th.

Judging by the reactions on this newsgroup to the handful of new cards in the
Sabbat War expansion, it would appear to me that veteran players are more than
capable of getting excited about "new toys" that interact with the existing
structure and are not set aside in their own little lonely corner of the game.
We are more than capable of get excited by Pier 13, Telepathic Tracking, City
Gangrel in sufficient numbers to make a deck out of, etc. etc.

For new players, of course, the old clans are a better draw. They represent
White Wolf's best creative efforts, are better developed, and more popular.
Any new players who are left cold by the old clans are unlikely to be drawn by
new ones.

>I also believe that adding new clans and disciplines, if/when it's
>done, must be done properly, so that we don't end up with the problems
>that the Ravnos, Giovanni, Assamites, and Setites had for so long.
>The two major weak points in the DS/AH expansions were:
>
>1) Not enough vampires, or vampires that sucked
>2) Not enough discipline cards that didn't suck

No argument here, except that for me, "done properly" includes the idea of
incorporating "new disciplines" as paths of existing disciplines..

>The "fragmentation" issue is one I'd like to save for later, since I
>have some pretty firm ideas but need to work up a solid basis to
>present them on.

Til then...

-- John Whelan

Hi yourself!

i've been keeping out of the debate about whether more clans and
disciplines is going to fragment the game too much, but when i was in
America i played a Cappadocian Happy Families deck quite a bit using
Damnan's new cards [accessible via Lasombra's site]. That deck slotted

Cappas really turned out to have a nice "flavour" about them. There were
certainly issues about some of the cards - Legion of Zombu is ridiculouly
over-powered, Temple of Erciyes needs tightening up textually, and the
reaction/combat/action modifier card that lets you not be burned from Agg

them.]

Why fragmentation didn't crop up as a problem perhaps bears some
examination. i think it's because the new cards for new disciplines
aren't really that new - they are version of cards used for other
disciplines, mostly, with a few little individual tweaks. Approached like

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
apologies in advance if i happen to match clan and discipline names
wrong, or if the clans I use aren't really related, or whatever. some
of this is off the top of my head.

On 13 Nov 2000 06:04:35 GMT, nys...@cs.com (Nystulc) wrote:

>it requires some clarification. My opinion expressed was that new disciplines
>would, *if* incorporated in the traditional V:tES manner damage the
>marketability of the game by fragmenting the customer base, and making it
>harder to satisfy the entire available customer base with each expansion. I

My first objection comes from this. Satisfying the entire existing
customer base is, frankly, a hopeless cause. There will always be
people unhappy with what has been done, and there will always be
people who think that something else should have been done. Any
number of companies have learned this the hard way, that you can't
make everyone happy all the time.

It is far more effective and profitable to make some people VERY
satisfied (by more narrowly targeting any new expansions). Players
are not going to get mad and quit just because the latest expansion
didn't have their favourite toys in; a good example is the lack of the
!Tremere in Sabbat War. Nobody is quitting because of it. Several
people are not thrilled with it, but they are also happy with the
-rest- of the expansion, so it works out.

>somewhere on the borders of survival. If the game ceases to be profitable,
>then it will not be marketted or promoted, and, in the long run, is likely to
>be less played. If the player base is fragmented, it becomes, for all
>practical purposes, smaller.

I question whether having a significant number of disciplines truly
"fragments" the player base. I have yet to have seen a single person
declare that they wouldn't be buying Sabbat War because their
favourite clan wasn't supported. Eleven clans WEREN'T supported in
SW; all the Camarilla, and all the Independents. All but four
disciplines got NO new cards whatsoever - and one discipline got only
Telepathic Tracking. Instead, the reaction has been nothing but
positive, enthusiastic, etc.

Having a wide number of disciplines helps to DIVERSIFY the player base
by encouraging variety, thus providing a greater number of people
actually playing the game. To say that more people playing is somehow
"smaller" is a fallacy, and so I must dispute your assertion. If we
have 200 people playing this game, and 100 of them buy the new
expansion, then we've sold 100. If we have 100 people playing this
game, and all of them buy the new expansion, we've still sold 100, but
we had no potential to sell more, and we still have fewer people
playing - a losing situation in the long run.

>>I can summarise my position thusly: I believe that adding new clans
>>and disciplines to the game is the ONLY WAY to guarantee a
>>consistently growing player base, because you MUST have a marketing
>>tie-in.
>
>This seems a very extreme position to take. I am confused as how adding new

Not especially. Stagnation = death. V:TES had nothing new for a long
time, and the player base shrunk enormously, even with the cheap
availability of the Jyhad base set to draw in the occasional new
player. Until you hit upon a 'classic' formula such as chess, then
ANYTHING must constantly be evolving with the times. This is a very
basic concept; if you don't have new stuff consistently, you will lose
out to the other, INFERIOR new stuff.

>clans and disciplines will assist in enhancing the player base, much less
>GUARANTEE such, much less be the ONLY such strategy worthy of consideration. I
>could be wrong, but I just cannot see how a V:tM player player will be
>convinced to try V:tES because of a new expansion introduces the new discipline
>of Spiritus, when they could not be lured by its featuring of Animalism,

Perhaps their "thing" happens to be Spiritus. Perhaps they've been
wondering about this V:TES thing for some time now, and when the White
Wolf marketing campaign hits the streets, it ends up being the final
push, and they go and get a box of the base V:TES set and a box of the
new expansion. I suspect you underestimate just how much marketing
potential is generated by "new and shiny", though. From what I
personally saw, Sabbat War has drawn a good bit of attention; not bad
for a dead game that just released a set consisting largely of
reprints. How did that happen? Marketing. New clans would provide a
huge potential, as everyone imagines the "cool powers" from each clan.

>Auspex, Celerity, Chimeristry, Dementate, Dominate, Fortitude, Necromancy,
>Obfuscate, Obtenebrate, Potence, Presence, Protean, Quietus, Serpentis,
>Thaumaturgy, or Vicissitude. Indeed, it seems more likely that the sheer
>number of clans and disciplines will intimidate new players (one of the reasons
>I favor focussed expansions).

If you present the game as "Thirteen clans and 21 disciplines!", then
yes, you're going to intimidate players. This would be a poor way to
present the game, though; a much better way would be to emphasize the
wide variety of clans you could play that you would also find in V:tM,
each of which has its inherent three disciplines. Remember, V:tM
players are already dealing with a wide variety of disciplines. It's
not going to bother them in the slightest, while finding that Mortis
has been relegated to merely a subset of Necromancy might.

As regards new players, the "starter deck" angle that WW is taking is
clearly intended to be the way to bring newer players into the game,
and looks to be very effective. You get your starter deck of a
cool-looking clan, then you buy some boosters to get some more cards
that fit with your clan, and you take the cards you don't want in the
boosters ("Protean? But the !Brujah don't have Protean...") and you
trade them away to other people for MORE cards that fit within your
clan and your deck. Eventually you get bored with the deck as you
become more familiar with the game, and you begin exploring different
options within the clan, and then different options OUTSIDE of the
clan, and so on, and so on.

New players will only be a problem if we try to hit them over the head
with everything at once, something WW's marketing group has rather
deftly avoided with the starter decks.

>Indeed, my concern was that any marginal gains in the player base made by such
>a strategy (if any) would be more than offset by the "fragmentation" of the
>interests of the existing customer base, such it would be more difficult to
>keep all players interested in every expansion. While the overall number of

as stated previously, the thought of keeping all players interested in
every expansion is hopeless. A much better approach is to ensure that
many players will be VERY interested in each expansion; an approach
that encourages DIVERSITY, not fragmentation.

>V:tES players MIGHT rise, a smaller percentage of these would be interested in
>each expansion, since its cards would be less likely to interact with those
>they prefer to play. For all practical purposes, fragmentation reduces the
>player base for each expansion.

The longer someone plays, the less likely they are to be satisfied
with "just one clan". I don't know anyone 'round here who's been
playing for any great length of time who still confines themselves to
any specific clan. The lure of the new (here it is again!) always
attracts them, and they build things and say "Well, I've never played
the Nosferatu before, but I figured I'd give them a try..."

About the only thing I've ever seen is the occasional player who
refuses to play one clan; will use all others EXCEPT one, frequently
Toreador. This, of course, hurts the game not at all.

>I do of course agree that new expansions are essential for marketing the game
>and keeping alive. I do not see why new disciplines MUST necessarily be part
>of this strategy.
>
>Of course, I am not against adding new things. Rather I am against adding new
>things in an unnecessarily fragmenting manner. Will introducing the "Mortis"
>the "new discipline" really have greater marketing value than introducing
>"Mortuus" the new set of powers for an old discipline? Thematically, they are
>virtually identical, so if one can be used for marketing, so can the other.

Virtually identical won't cut it. Surely you've seen the complaints
regarding Wake with Evening's Freshness and how it should be a
Tremere-only card? We all know that for game balance, it wouldn't
work, since everyone needs to have the -capability- to untap. But
people still bitch about it.

Also, YES, the name-recognition matters enormously. "Mortis" is
something that V:tM players are familiar with. "Cappadocians" are
something they're familiar with. Splashing out advertising that touts
the Cappadocians in the next expansion and a bunch of Mortis cards
will snag the eye of V:tM players in a huge way. Splashing out
advertising that gives the new "Mortuus" path to Necromancy ...
well... you lose the name recognition, and probably confuse people.
The first question they'll ask is "Why didn't they just call it
Mortis?", and then they'll complain about the Cappadocians not having
Necromancy itself at all, and so on and so on. Name recognition is an
extremely important part of advertising - why do you think products
will go out of their way to never specifically name their competitors?
The Coke/Pepsi wars are a very rare situation, where both brands have
sufficient name recognition on their own. In general, though, you
want to capitalize on any "name" you've gone out of your way to
establish. So yes, "Mortis" the new is much more valuable than
"Mortuus", the weird Necromancy variant.

>>Some people love the Gangrel, true, and adding the occasional
>>new toy for the Gangrel is great... but the Gangrel are quite viable
>>the way they are, and there's no need to screw with that. Taking a
>>brand-new clan and simply making them a subset of a previous clan and
>>a previous discipline just won't thrill people. The average person
>>wants New n' Shiny, and a New Clan with New Toys is it.
>
>I presume you are talking about veteran players here, who have already
>collected all the "old Toys". It seems to me difficult to believe that any
>player fanatic enough to have collected cards from all 22 clans and all 17
>disciplines, in numbers sufficient to be playable, will somehow lose interest
>and stop playing just because he does not get a 23rd and a 18th.

I am not. I am speaking of newer players who we are trying to draw
in. See above for why "new n' shiny" matters so much; it's been in a
couple different paragraphs.

>Judging by the reactions on this newsgroup to the handful of new cards in the
>Sabbat War expansion, it would appear to me that veteran players are more than
>capable of getting excited about "new toys" that interact with the existing
>structure and are not set aside in their own little lonely corner of the game.
>We are more than capable of get excited by Pier 13, Telepathic Tracking, City
>Gangrel in sufficient numbers to make a deck out of, etc. etc.

Yes, because we've all been watching for several years now as
equipment has continued to suck, S:CE has continued to make combat
suck, and the City Gangrel were a totally lost cause due to lack of
vampires. We are happy, ...because we have new things, emphasizing my
points above about "new and shiny".

>For new players, of course, the old clans are a better draw. They represent
>White Wolf's best creative efforts, are better developed, and more popular.
>Any new players who are left cold by the old clans are unlikely to be drawn by
>new ones.

One of the reasons I advocated that the next expansion after final
nights be a reprint of the base set, to attempt to draw totally
brand-new players who are not familiar with V:tM or the World of
Darkness at all. Also, such players who are not drawn to the 'older'
clans at all will likely never play the game anyway, and so are
largely irrelevant.

>>I also believe that adding new clans and disciplines, if/when it's
>>done, must be done properly, so that we don't end up with the problems
>>that the Ravnos, Giovanni, Assamites, and Setites had for so long.
>>The two major weak points in the DS/AH expansions were:
>>
>>1) Not enough vampires, or vampires that sucked
>>2) Not enough discipline cards that didn't suck
>
>No argument here, except that for me, "done properly" includes the idea of
>incorporating "new disciplines" as paths of existing disciplines..

Well... here's the problem with that, as I see it. All the
marketing/etc. ideas aside, assume you create a new clan, the
Cappadocians, and a new discipline, Mortis. Jolly. I'll go ahead and
use the Gangrel as a "baseline", since they are a well-developed clan
who possess a discipline, Protean, which was unique to them when they
were introduced. From looking at the site with the created
Cappadocian cards, their skill set seems to be MOR/AUS/FOR.

The Gangrel have 21 discipline cards, 11 "clan toy" cards of some
form, and 24 vampires. This is after one set and three expansions,
keep in mind. The original Jyhad Gangrel only had 10 discipline cards
and 7 "clan toys"; I don't remember how many vamps. Oh, and a skill
card "Protean", so call it 8/12 clan toys.

To make the Cappadocians viable, you need to print 12 vampires and
10-15 discipline cards for Mortis. You should print at least 8 clan
toys in some form; this means that 30-35 cards of your new expansion
are going to be totally focussed on Cappadocians. If you introduce
two new clans in one expansion (reference DS and AH), then you have 70
cards of your expansion, worst case, that are totally about the new
clans. Assuming a 120 card expansion, since that's a number I've seen
tossed around a lot, then that still leaves you 50 cards to totally
and gratuitously screw around with; so you shouldn't have problems
throwing a bone or two to everyone else in the set, say 2 new cards
for every other old discipline, leaving you 24 cards... then 2 new
vamps for each of the Independents and the Sabbat clans, with Mortis
and/or the other new discipline on them, takes you right down to 2
cards left. I excluded the "original 7" because right now, they have
significantly more vampires than any other clan out there, even after
Sabbat War; we need to bring the existing stuff up to speed.
Hopefully Final Nights will help with that, and we can begin adding
more toys for the original 7.

Anyway, this certainly seems to indicate that it's no problem to
include plenty of support for the "veteran" players in a new
expansion; when 50 out of 120 cards are related to existing clans,
it's highly likely that even if someone doesn't want the Cappadocians,
they'll get some of the new expansion for the other-discipline stuff.
So while it's still not possible to make EVERYONE happy (some people
will undoubtedly bitch about having to buy the stupid Cappadocians
just to get the cool new Auspex cards), you certainly don't leave very
many people out.

Now, to address the problem with making Mortis a subset of Necromancy,
and the Cappadocians a subset of ... the Giovanni? I don't remember
how you intended to handle that *exactly*, so correct me if I mess up
somewhere.

To symbolise the Cappadocians properly, I assume you would be printing
"Cappadocian" text on the vampires, while still using the Giovanni
clan symbol and background, so that they could benefit from the
existing Giovanni hunting grounds, etc. OK. I also must assume that
you would be creating a number of vampires with NEC/AUS/FOR in some
variant. Fair enough. I believe you've then said that you would
print Mortis cards by using the NEC symbol, and specifying somehow on
the card "requires a Cappadocian".

This, however, creates a number of potential balance issues that will
rapidly become difficult to resolve, as well as some thematic/style
issues.

First, as tempting as it may be to just think of the Cappadocians as a
"subset" of the Giovanni, they've been deliberately separated in the
World of Darkness, and you lose most of the marketing draw for Mortis.
There's also the confusion that is generated by having an elaborate
setup to distinguish between clans, while to the casual onlooker the
vampires in question are all of the same clan; why weren't THESE just
done up separately like all the rest? Loses style points. Also loses
style points for complicated-ness; when you have to include "Only
playable by a Cappadocian" on NEC skill cards, you no longer have the
visual reference that the skill symbols were intended to provide.
Newer players will be rapidly confused as to why the card in their
hand with the discipline symbol their vampire has isn't playable, and
will become frustrated. Speaking of frustrated, skill cards... how do
you add Mortis to vampires? "This Vampire is a Cappadocian" cards?

Second, the game balance issues become very difficult. By making
Cappadocians have NEC, you effectively give them four disciplines;
Mortis, Auspex, Fortitude, and Necromancy. Any Necromancy cards you
print are not automatically restricted to the "true" Giovanni, as they
could normally be; the Cappadocians have them too, so now you must
print Giovanni-only cards instead of making them discipline-related.
Some card combinations may become an immediate issue; is there a
reason that NEC/AUS shouldn't be combined together at such a low
level? How about NEC/FOR? Is Minion Tap/Force of Will/Possession too
powerful? Maybe not, but what else haven't you thought of? Players
are creative... they'll discover things to do with old cards that the
playtesters will overlook. Do we need more AUS/FOR vampires? How
about the Giovanni clan toys? Ambrosius, eww... do the Cappadocians
need Ambrosius?

(This is one of the things that worries me about the Gargoyles people
are mentioning; POT/PRO is one of the discipline combos that doesn't
need to show up too easily, especially in the form POT/pro.
POT/PRO/FOR could be even worse. Bleeds for 1 are still pretty damn
effective, and there's always Computer Hacking once you're done
burning all his vampires. Some disciplines DO NOT need to be
combined, because of the existing cards.)

So, what happens is you end up restricting the Mortis cards too
carefully, or worse, not carefully enough. If you had separated the
discipline out, you wouldn't have to worry about the game balance
issues as much, although you'd still have to ask yourself whether or
not the game needed more AUS/FOR vampires. But by separating Mortis,
you gain a significant number of benefits, some tangible, some
intangible. Right now, there is already an AUS/FOR clan, so you can
pretty much assume that AUS/FOR, as a combination, doesn't pose a
significant problem to game balance. This gives you great flexibility
with creating the Mortis cards, as unless you're quite careless, you
have difficulty "breaking" the game. I tried looking at Damnans' page
to go through his proposed Mortis cards, and it's not showing up right
for some reason. But really, no matter what route you take with
Mortis, whether you make it a bleed discipline, a combat discipline, a
utility discipline, what have you, it's MUCH easier to maintain
balance when you can separate it somewhat. Legbiter played his
Cappadocian deck several times during his visit, and I never felt that
it was HORRIBLY broken, even though Damnans' vampires and his cards
are noticeably high-powered. (The Legion of Zombu, however, is just a
no-no from the word "go".)

And just because it's partly separate doesn't mean that it has to be
TOTALLY off in its own world. The Ventrue Anti would undoubtedly be
happy to get another few AUS/FOR vampires, to supplement themselves.
There are several mono-FOR decks, and plenty of mono-Auspex decks that
would be delighted to get the new low-cap vamps. Depending on what
"fourth-discipline" skills you scattered among the clan, you could
easily provide some support to the Toreador (include some inferior
Presence), the Ravnos/Gangrel/Tzimisce (include some Animalism),
Malkavians (include some Obfuscate), ... take your pick.

(whew) OK. Breathing now.



Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 12 Nov 2000 11:17:01 -0500, Derek Ray wrote:

>So you got out Arika, Minion Tapped her down to 6, and bled with this
>card. Day Op for unblockable, and Conditioning for a bleed modifier
>afterwards; total bleed amount = 3 + 11 + 3 = 17.

A five card combo; how shocking. In this case, I'd point the finger
at Minion Tap. The more I see of this card, the cheesier it seems.

>Several different errata were tried, and none really proved useful, as
>you had to be playing combat *and* get through an Obedience wall in
>order to actually remove blood from the vampire in question and negate
>the card. The NJL tried "no action modifiers may be played with this
>card", so you couldn't Day Op or add stealth to it, but this left the
>door open for the Concoction of Vitality and Marked Path.

A counter card like Shadowfist's Expendable Unit is one possibility -
a card which would make a minion take the hit instead of you being
bled. And make it disciplineless so that it's more generally
available than Deflection. That's rather like the Mile Away
suggestion but a bit pricier - you'd have to sacrifice a minion to
stop a big bleed.

The errata that I'd like to see tried is to make X (the value of the
bleed) equal to the amount of blood on the acting vampire rather than
its capacity. This would reduce the value of the bleed by at least 4
(the cost of the action) and increase the overall cost of the action
considerably by stopping the abusive Minion Tap combo. And most
importantly, it would do little violence to the original wording.

Andrew

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 12 Nov 2000 12:49:21 -0500, Derek Ray wrote:

>First, only something like seven cards have been banned. A pretty
>good track record, since most of them have OBVIOUS problems in
>tournament play.

It's a lousy track record. Most CGG don't ban any cards while this
game just apes Magic and continues to use DCI rules.

>How do you deal with Madness of the Bard, for example?

> ...

>So you have to ban the card. There's no other way.

I'm feel sure that the card was banned because the PTB didn't like it,
not because it's impossible to play. They're second guessing the
designer - that's what stinks about all these errata and bans. Not
being prepared to play the game as it is but insisting on shaping it
to their own vision of how it ought to have been.

>Return to Innocence does not need to be revitalized. It needs to be
>gone, and stay gone. The game was not designed to handle bleeds of
>10-15 from a single vampire in one action.

It seems clear that Return to Innocence was explicitly designed to let
you make a big bleed at the cost of a vampire. The game is not a
platonic ideal - it is merely the sum of its parts and RtI is one of
those parts. If you ban RtI or MoB, you're not playing the game as
designed and printed. This is a greater sacrilege than playing with a
card limit.

>Most combat decks couldn't afford the 8 Wakes and 8 copies of your

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 12 Nov 2000 12:49:21 -0500, Derek Ray wrote:

>Some cards are sufficiently broken that immediate repair is required.
>(see: RtI) This is V:TES, not Magic.

It seems almost indistinguishable from Magic to me - they ban and
errata cards at the drop of a hat too. Now that the game is free of
WotC, I'd like to see the DCI mentality shed so that the game can
develop its own identity.

>How do you deal with Madness of the Bard, for example? Aside from the
>problems it causes for non-native-language speakers, it relies on a
>totally subjective interpretation of what a "rhyme" is. No two people
>are likely to agree. One person on here believes that simply
>repeating the sentence twice qualifies as a rhyme; I would NEVER
>permit such a thing as a judge, but that just points up the real
>problem with the card, that it's totally dependent on who's judging.
>
>So you have to ban the card. There's no other way.

What rot. The card could use some clarification but it is certainly
playable. The card reads "All players in the game must speak in
rhyming sentences." Presumably this means that each player must speak
in rhyming couplets. In particular, the sentences are not required to
rhyme internally (the rain in spain...); players are not required to
rhyme with each other; and that the rhyme can start afresh after each
pair (i.e. couplets). Requiring formal grammatical sentences seems
too fussy and I'd be happy with terse stuff like "Yes. I guess." as a
valid couplet.

Repetition is a cheesy way of getting round the requirement but
certainly obeys the letter of the law. Note that there are plenty of
real poems which make good use of repetition, e.g. Old MacDonald or
The Raven. If the card saw heavy use then I'd expect some standard
boilerplate devices of this kind to develop. You can see this in game
shows like Jeopardy. US natives probably take this for granted
through long familiarity but I find it amusingly bizarre that the
requirement that each answer must be phrased as a question has
degenerated to just adding "What is" on the front of the real answer.

UK residents will be more familiar with the game show, "Just a Minute"
in which the contestants must talk on a random subject for up to a
minute without "hesitation, deviation or repetition." They are
allowed to repeat the subject title but it's obviously not sporting to
repeatedly chant this alone and this would normally be challenged as
deviation. It's a great game and easily played at any time without
any equipment except a stop watch. It's scored just like VTES - if
you oust the speaker with a succesful challenge you score a point and
you get a final VP if you have the floor when the minute is up.

While we're at it, can someone explain why the Monocle of Clarity of
banned too? This all reminds me of the cartoon in which Dogbert frees
Dilbert from the trolls of the accounting department by threatening to
turn his cap backwards and so make their hard-wired brains explode.
In the final frame, Dilbert asks, "what's that sound?" and Dogbert
explains, "a paradigm shifting without a clutch."

Andrew

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 13 Nov 2000 19:41:47 +0000, Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com>
wrote:

>On Sun, 12 Nov 2000 11:17:01 -0500, Derek Ray wrote:
>
>>So you got out Arika, Minion Tapped her down to 6, and bled with this
>>card. Day Op for unblockable, and Conditioning for a bleed modifier
>>afterwards; total bleed amount = 3 + 11 + 3 = 17.
>
>A five card combo; how shocking. In this case, I'd point the finger
>at Minion Tap. The more I see of this card, the cheesier it seems.

And you would be in error. The problem is not the 5 blood gained from
Minion Tapping an IC member; the problem is the bleed for 17. Return
to Innocence is no less broken just because it cost someone an 11-pool
vampire instead of a 6-pool vampire.

Minion Tap is also one of the few cards that makes large vampires
worth playing; when you can get out a 10-cap and immediately pull 6
back from it, you are at far less risk if someone happens to Rush,
Pentex Subvert, Sensory Deprive, or otherwise pull off any of the
"screw one vampire" tricks that are very prevalent in the game.
Changing or removing Minion Tap would tip the balance far towards
weenies.

The *true* blood-gain cheese with Minion Tap comes when it's combined
with a single vampire and 5th Tradition. And in this instance, it's
been suggested repeatedly that errata to 5th Tradition requiring that
it be used on a -different- vampire would be a good step towards a
solution for the MT/5th combo; no more getting out Emerson and having
him MT/5th as his first action.

>>Several different errata were tried, and none really proved useful, as
>>you had to be playing combat *and* get through an Obedience wall in
>>order to actually remove blood from the vampire in question and negate
>>the card. The NJL tried "no action modifiers may be played with this
>>card", so you couldn't Day Op or add stealth to it, but this left the
>>door open for the Concoction of Vitality and Marked Path.
>
>A counter card like Shadowfist's Expendable Unit is one possibility -
>a card which would make a minion take the hit instead of you being
>bled. And make it disciplineless so that it's more generally
>available than Deflection. That's rather like the Mile Away
>suggestion but a bit pricier - you'd have to sacrifice a minion to
>stop a big bleed.

First problem: what do you do about Big Vampire Decks that include 20
copies of this card and just soak up any bleeds with a 10-cap
Prince/Justicar who does nothing but 5th Tradition himself every turn,
sit there, and cast his votes?

Second problem: by making it disciplineless, you turn it into a
replacement for most other bleed defenses, neutering bleed
significantly as a strategy.

Third problem: you need to carefully design the card so that people
are only able to play it with minions who have enough blood to cover
the bleed, otherwise you give weenie decks yet another enormous
benefit ("Smudge lobs himself in the way of that bleed for 6. Aw, he
goes to torpor, he only had 1. Rats"). Once you do that, this makes
the card itself somewhat worthless for the NON-big vampire decks.

Fourth problem: you mandate that everyone have and obtain this card
or be ousted by RtI. Again, it degenerates into an "X or anti-X"
problem, and that's been accepted as a Bad Thing.

>The errata that I'd like to see tried is to make X (the value of the
>bleed) equal to the amount of blood on the acting vampire rather than
>its capacity. This would reduce the value of the bleed by at least 4
>(the cost of the action) and increase the overall cost of the action
>considerably by stopping the abusive Minion Tap combo. And most
>importantly, it would do little violence to the original wording.

This has been suggested, and is a logical errata. I don't recall if
it was tried or not, but it still leaves the door open for pesky Soul
Gem combinations. Once you errata the "burn" to "remove from the
game", then you are in better shape, but now you're doing more
violence to the card text.

Actually, thinking back, I believe it WAS tried, and it was concluded
that being hit for a 12-point bleed with Arika was pretty much just as
bad as being hit for a 17-point bleed. To add insult to injury, of
course, there was using one of the 10-cap Justicars instead, who would
just MT/5th himself once beforehand, and then come and whack you for
10.

Bleeds of that size from one vampire, no matter what the source,
simply do not belong in the game. RtI effectively turns the game into
a "bounce or die" situation, and it becomes a contest of who can draw
their RtI first.

Messages.Author: Pat Ricochet
Messages.Body:
> This is not the only solution. You can create hosers which have
> sufficient general utility that they are common in the metagame and so
> deter use of the power card.

In the words of George Carlin, "This sentence is full of things that
piss me off." No actual offense met, though; replace "piss me off" with
"worry me."

"You can create hosers..."
1) ...that people have to have in their deck, or die. This gets to the
'Play X or anti-X' issue, which makes all the rest of the cards cute, but no
good for winning; either in your playgroup, if you have a player just only
has fun by winning, or in tournaments, where the point is to Win. After
winning a tournament, some people move on to Winning With Style or just
Having Fun, but the tournament will reduce to 'Play X or anti-X' and drive
people away. I'm personally not sure I was ever going to play in a
tournament again after seeing tap-and-bleed win Dragon*Con. Thanks to
Misdirection being *fixed*, proving to me that errata can be a Very Very
Good Thing, I'm once again excited about tournament play.

"...which have sufficient general utility..."
2) ...that no deck can or should be without them. This is a subset of 'Play
X or anti-X.' No CCG should have The Card you have to have to be
competitive. It's fine to have Good Cards that go well in almost any deck,
but 'sufficient general utility' can just wallpaper other cards.

"...that they are common in the metagame..."
3) ...so common, in fact, that everyone will have them, so no one will play
the card(s) they're protecting against. Which, in effect, is the same as
banning the offending card. If they're NOT that common, then we're back to
point #1, that if someone is playing a card like Return to Innocence, either
they will be hosed by the "hoser" of "sufficient general utility," and RtI
is worthless, or they won't be stopped by the hoser card, and then RtI will
crush the poor sap who didn't have The Hoser Card in hand. (note that be
needing it "in hand" they, and everyone else, is required to have MANY
copies of The Hoser Card.

<soapbox>
"...and so deter the use of the power card."
4) Ok, I'll admit that the words "...the power card" falls into the 'piss me
off' category more than the 'annoy me' category. MtCH can have their "power
cards," but keep them away from my beloved V:tES. The game was not meant to
have a single card that if you got it could dominate or win you the game,
and the errata may be, as was argued against, be the needs and feelings of
the rules team over the needs and feeling of the designers. If the designer
of RtI was designing a "power card," and this generation of V:tES players is
mature enough to want a more thought out and planned and strategic game,
where you win through a culmination of many clever tricks and plays, and not
just one card, GOOD. There will always be a "final blow" as someone is
ousted, sometimes an anticlimactic bleed for one, sometimes a magnificent
table-mangaged vote with a side-effect no one noticed but the scheming
Methuselah calling the vote...which makes for the great "war stories" V:tES
players have. "And then I bled with Arika for 13 and ousted him!" isn't the
kind of victory most V:tES players want. Sure, it's cute...once. But that
doesn't keep the immature, uncreative players from abusing it over and over
and over. If banning such cards drives away players wanting "power card"
options to them, so be it. Maybe banning/errata of "power cards" isn't the
best way to address the issues of all CCGs, but it sure is the best way for
a strategic balanced game like V:tES.
</soapbox>

--
Pat Ricochet
Soul Jar'rn Fool of Atlanta

Andrew S. Davidson <a...@csi.com> wrote:

>Innocence gives you a killer punch but it's not clear that it sets you
>up well to sweep the table because the large vampire that did it is
>burned.

Untrue. Consider the Etrius Happy Fun Ball Deck, which I made (way back in the
days when RtoI was new)explicitly to showcase RtoI's overarching advantage:

Crypt

12xEtrius (11 AUS DOM OBF pro THA)

Library
20xReturn to Innocence
10xHorrific Countenance
10xDay Operation
20xSoul Gem of Etrius
20xFortitude
10xFreak Drive

Fairly straightforward: Get out Etrius. Give him Fortitude. Equip with Soul
Gem. Freak Drive. Return to Innocence/Day Operation for a bleed of 14.
Etrius burns, Soul Gem kicks in, get a fresh Etrius. Next turn, give Etrius
Fortitude, Return to Innocence, Day Operation for a bleed of 14. Etrius
burns, Soul Gem kicks in, get a fresh Etrius. 12 Etrii in the crypt, each
bleeding for 14 = 172 pool, more than enough to oust the 30 pool of each
of your four opponents, never mind what they've expended on vampires of
their own.

And that isn't even tuned. The deck can be made strong vs. combat by adding
10 Obediences, or even fewer. It's not particularly vulnerable to vote or
bleed. And it bleeds unblockably for 14. Every turn. Replace RtoI with
Govern the Unaligned, and it's an amusing joke -- the whole point is to burn
the bleeding vampire. The cost of RtoI has been turned into an asset.

Such decks force everyone to play with bleedbounce, Protected Resources, or
Archon Investigation. This either circumscribes the game environment severely
(bad) or forces everyone to chase hard-to-find, expensive rare cards (worse).

And it all hinges -- exclusively -- on Return to Innocence, because it's so
damned efficient. One card packs a massive wallop with a cost that some
creative deckbuilding can turn into an asset. Banning seven cards out of
1300 or so is hardly 'wholesale banning,' as you've asserting, and comparing
sane rules changes for the sake of balance is hardly equivalent to a card
limit, as you've ludicrously asserted elsewhere. VTES is a better and more
playable game today that it was when it was printed, and that difference
comes from the care and attention given to post-release tuning.

gomi

> >good track record, since most of them have OBVIOUS problems in
> >tournament play.
>
> It's a lousy track record. Most CGG don't ban any cards while this
> game just apes Magic and continues to use DCI rules.

It's a great track record. Anyone who thinks a complex game can be
published without players finding the occasional weakness in the
rules is basically mad. Weak components of games should be fixed;
not allowed to sit and fester. Jyhad is just like any other game.
Over time, certain rules have been found to be incomplete, self-
contradictory, and/or unclear. And certain strategies have been
found to be imbalanced, which causes serious problems since such
imbalance general precludes the pursuit of many, MANY other paths to
victories which the designers had put a lot of time and effort into
creating for the game.

Under the circumstances, it's not surprising that the rules get
changed. Third Reich, I understand, has undergone many changes over
the years to clean up various aspects of the game which didn't
work correctly. With a board game, you simple republish it and
people who want it can buy the new copy or mock up their old
components to follow the new rules. With CCGs, you just reissue
any new rules which don't affect cards directly. However, you
must remember that the non-flavor text written on cards are part of
the rules of the game as well, and when you need to rewrite these
part of the rules, the rewrite comes in the form of errata. If the
new rule is to simply not allow the card in question because its
rules are not worth fixing, then the card is banned.

Given how complicated a game Jyhad, the banning of only seven cards for
tournament purposes is fantastic. As for those other games, I can't
say. I've heard tell that the designers of a lot of other games just
stupidly don't care about play-balance hardly at all and ignore
imbalance, with predicable results. If that's what you're holding
up as the ideal, you can keep it.

Fred

"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:
> Rediscovering this game is bringing back ugly memories of Magic. You
> see the differences - I see the similarities.

Ironically, your point of view brings back *my* ugly memories of Magic.
And Jyhad, for that matter. I played for years beginning with the first
sanctioned tournaments in 1994. I was a top 25 DCI player in 1994 and
1995, back when the ratings system granted points for simply attending
tournaments and stair-stepped upwards for each round of the single
elimination tournaments you advanced through. (Losing in the first round
got you 10 points. If you won the first round and lost the second, you
got 10 + 20 for a total of 30 points. Losing in the third round counted
60 points, and so on. Player ranking positions were determined by total
points accumulated throughout a one year period.) I wasn't that good of
a player. Fair, I suppose, but no genius. I attended a lot of
tournaments. But mostly, I had "The "Jewels". The power 9 probably won
me a lot more matches than my playing savvy. As a fair contest of skill,
it was just silly.

It took WotC years to accept the fact that I could see plain and simple
myself that power cards kill a constructed deck game. And it also took
years before the playing community began to grasp that point, either. I
argued with so many idiots in Magic newsgroups who kept getting lost at
around the point of reason that a card does not have to be overwhelmingly
powerful to harm a game. Merely being way more powerful than most cards
will do, even if hosers for it exist. Even now, Type 1 only exists because
it has a character to it that certain kinds of players like. They don't
care about the fact that many, many cards are basically worthless in Type I
as much as they like the speed and dynamics of the game. They're entitled
to their preferences, I suppose. But they're in the distinct minority for
a good reason.

As for Jyhad, until it was turned over to LSJ, I feel that WotC was in
total denial about the importance of play balance. Though I understand
the discomfort with the shear amount of errata that LSJ has issued to fix
the various problems he sees, there's no doubt in my mind that the game is
in far better shape today than it was before he took over.

Fred

No - that's why tournaments have to have a Judge. The tournament
rules on stalling, collusion and sportsmanship are subjective. So too
are many more subtle points such as whether a player did or did not
declare an action. I gather that Magic play at the highest levels
turns on such minute details and that a judge has to monitor the
behaviour of each player very closely. The more seriously you take a
game, the more you have to confront such issues. Just look at the US
Presidential election. In theory, this is a simple matter of counting
votes. In practise, it is turning on all sorts of subjective,
physical details like whether a chad is pregnant or not. Can you call
for a recount in a VTES referendum <grin>?

>V:TES is a game about deck-building and play of the cards and

James (Legbiter) McClellan has so cleverly pointed out, the card
itself indicates that repetition is a valid rhyme and this option is
available to any speaker, whatever their mother tongue. This does not
make the card useless - it just makes the challenge more subtle.

Suppose you adopt the simple ruse of ending each sentence with the
word "period". This mannerism is common in ordinary US speech and
seems to be the perfect way of punctuating each sentence in a rhyming
way. This sounds easy but the catch is that you have to remember to
do it. Those familiar with the Shadowfist card, "Art of War", will
know how hard this can be.

>You still have not yet satisfactorily answered the question of what to
>do with non-native speakers.

See above.

>And he's screwed, because he HAS to be able to communicate to the rest
>of us somehow what he wants. Similarly, I would be screwed were I to
>play with his group in Poland, as I can't even say his NAME correctly,
>much less make a rhyme in his language.

The VEKN rules say nothing about the language to be used in an event
though, as the rules and cards only exist in English form, there is an
implicit presumption that any player must be fluent and literate in
that language. This is a general issue at events such as the European
Championships. You seem to think that a player can insist that a
particular language must be used but what would it be in this case -
German, English or what? Maybe we need a set of sign-cards for
international events - in the same way as football referees have to
use coloured cards and arm signals.

Andrew
