using a Madness Network at the end of their predator's minion phase, so the
pile of errata makes no difference, since no one else (except other Bum's
Rushing Malks, I guess) has any chance to see it coming, rush, deal, etc.
So the card was errata'd *again*, and now says:
"You play this this card at any time. This card is removed from the
game, and is not to ever be put back into your deck, or any other deck."

and the flavor text says something like

"For an even larger collection of bookmarks inspired by poor design,
insufficient playtesting, clever blokes who broke the cards, and cheezball
players who would play them in tournaments, go to
http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/banned"

>> It's like most threads on this group, the old guys remember how bad it
>> was. Most like it as it is now. Opinions and experience are different
>> animals Andrew.
>

> Rediscovering this game is bringing back ugly memories of Magic. You
> see the differences - I see the similarities.

We see the differences (I say "we" only because I haven't seen anyone
else poke up defending Return to Broken Cards..er, Innocence) in the history
of how long and how many broken cards were allowed in Magic, where V:tES is
self-repairing to keep open the wide variety of strategies to all be
competitive.
You seem to see the similarity that Magic banned cards, and "all banning
of cards is a bad thing". You've certainly never answered again on the idea
that the game designers CAN and HAVE made mistakes in designing cards. You
attribute more credit to the wisdom of one group of people (the original
designers) that some other group of people (the rules team). Hindsight is
20/20, and that means the errata are made with more knowledge and experience
(thereby, wisdom) than the original designers had.
But, it's not a matter of blind trust. We can see for ourselves, by
actually playing the game and the cards, seeing tournaments with all the
same broken trick winning all the VPs, that "this card" or "that card" is
broken, and unbalances an otherwise excellent game.
We are very fortunate to have LSJ at the helm, who manages to keep the
"letter of the law" clear even in the most obtuse situations, and who keeps
to the "spirit of the law" in issuing errata to preserve the balanced nature
of the game.
The difference, to many players, is that (most all) Magic players like
only to win, and (most all) V:tES players actually like to *play*. We like
the game, we like the variety, we like the complexity that amazingly retains
an excellent set of checks and balances. And we want to *keep* it that way.
*That* is what matters most to us. What seems to matter most to you is
cards not be changed, and certainly not banned.
As you say:

> Leaving ante cards aside, this now only has three banned cards to VTES's four.
> This makes VTES the worst CCG in this respect, worse even than Magic.
> Shameful.

I find the idea of four banned cards being "shameful" to be bizarre,
really. I can't fathom why it bothers you so much.
Play balance matters to me. It's part of what attracted me to V:tES,
(the other half being the complexity, and the montage of having that much
complexity while still being play balanced is what makes V:tES shine.) and
it certainly matters to me far *more* than whether 4 or 3 or 0 cards out of
Oodles got banned.

All that contrariness aside, lemme say one thing in some agreement. I'm
not sure it's clear that Rowan Ring needs to be banned, really, considering
the amount of errata that is in existence. "Paralyze" got nixed a long time
ago, but Wooden stake got fixed, and I can't think it's too hard to make
text for Rowan Ring that does the intended purpose. I mean, there is the
Amaranth/Archon combo, or just use Amaranth with Mua-cheeze, but is that
really a "broken" combo?

That is, indeed, the very volume, another of whose highlights is the
revelation that Ulugh Beg was a Tuba during playtesting.

Not particularly wanting to rake over old ashes here, but i do want to
comment briefly on the [as i see it] validity of the general point that
Andrew is making, which is that text-unsupported errata are INCREDIBLY
annoying for new/returning players. i think everyone knows this, and the
question really becomes, which is more important: [1] keeping the game
transparent so that new people can basically pick up a deck, read the
rules, and play; or [2] keeping the game balanced, so that particular
cards and strategies don't achieve a boring degree of dominance in
tournaments/general competitive play. The NG has a view on this which is
basically that [2] wins out, but i have a foot in another camp of Playing
for Fun with family and friends. There, the parlour-game nature of MotB
is actually an ATTRACTIVE feature of the card and many of them simply
don't understand [2] and think it is elitist crap.

In the future i would like to see problem cards quite simply BANNED from
tournaments, just as the problem strategy of repeat actions is BANNED
from tournaments, rather than the issuing of text-unsupported errata. And
the justification for the banning would quite simply be that the Rules
Team have banned it, or that the Judges don't think they can cope with
enforcing the play of the card. Cards could be unbanned later, though,
when they are reissued with modified text.

Messages.Author: John Whelan
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 13 Nov 2000, Derek Ray wrote:

> My first objection comes from this. Satisfying the entire existing
> customer base is, frankly, a hopeless cause. There will always be
> people unhappy with what has been done, and there will always be
> people who think that something else should have been done. Any
> number of companies have learned this the hard way, that you can't
> make everyone happy all the time.

I agree that 100% absolute customer satisfaction is impossible. It does
not thereby follow, of course, that customer satisfaction does not matter,
and that such factors can be ignored. Your objection is inadequate. You
have dodged the issue of whether fragmentation reduces customer
satisfaction, and gone on to argue points that are not under contention.

> It is far more effective and profitable to make some people VERY
> satisfied (by more narrowly targeting any new expansions).

I am in favor of focussed expansions. There is no disagreement here.

> Players
> are not going to get mad and quit just because the latest expansion
> didn't have their favourite toys in;

No. If they feel they do not get adequate reward for the money they
spend, they are more likely to get bored and quit. They will drift
away. I don't expect grand speeches from the vast majority of people who
stop playing.

> a good example is the lack of the
> !Tremere in Sabbat War.

A move that I approve of. I had in fact stated, before the release, that
it would be good if as many as two or three clans were left out in the
interest of adequate focus.

> Nobody is quitting because of it.

You mean nobody is suddenly quitting because of it after making loud
speaches of protest. People are quitting, of course, for one reason or
another. Presumably they drift away because they find more rewarding ways
to spend their time and money. Giving them less satisfaction for their
money is an excellent way to ensure that we lose the competition for their
interests.

> Several
> people are not thrilled with it, but they are also happy with the
> -rest- of the expansion, so it works out.

Once more clans and disciplines exist, you will have to leave out even
more clans and disciplines to make an expansion adequately focussed. This
is because, even though the number of clans/disciplines increases, the
number that can be reasonably featured in an adequately focussed expansion
remains the same.

So several more people will be even less thrilled with it. I am
impressed by your amazing faith that no-one will ever stop playing on
this account.

> >somewhere on the borders of survival. If the game ceases to be profitable,
> >then it will not be marketted or promoted, and, in the long run, is likely to
> >be less played. If the player base is fragmented, it becomes, for all
> >practical purposes, smaller.
>
> I question whether having a significant number of disciplines truly
> "fragments" the player base. I have yet to have seen a single person
> declare that they wouldn't be buying Sabbat War because their
> favourite clan wasn't supported.

I doubt that you spend much time talking to people who no longer play the
game. In any event, the players who still play, who have not lost
interest and drifted to other games, are those fanatics like you or I who
have continued to collect and play the game for the past 4 years in spite
of the level of fragmentation already introduced. It is unlikely that any
such people will suddently stop playing in loud protest after the first
expansion that does NOT increase the fragmentation level.

> Eleven clans WEREN'T supported in
> SW; all the Camarilla, and all the Independents. All but four
> disciplines got NO new cards whatsoever - and one discipline got only
> Telepathic Tracking. Instead, the reaction has been nothing but
> positive, enthusiastic, etc.

Yes indeed, from us hardcore fanatics who have been continued to play this
game for the last 4 years with little or no support from WoTC and no
expansions.

> Having a wide number of disciplines helps to DIVERSIFY the player base
> by encouraging variety, thus providing a greater number of people
> actually playing the game.

And how exactly does it do this?

> To say that more people playing is somehow
> "smaller" is a fallacy, and so I must dispute your assertion.

When you rephrase it in so ingenious a manner, how can I disagree?

> If we
> have 200 people playing this game, and 100 of them buy the new
> expansion, then we've sold 100. If we have 100 people playing this
> game, and all of them buy the new expansion, we've still sold 100, but
> we had no potential to sell more, and we still have fewer people
> playing - a losing situation in the long run.

You seem to be suggesting that by doubling the number of clans we can
double (or at least substantially increase) the number of players. I

> setup to distinguish between clans, while to the casual onlooker the
> vampires in question are all of the same clan; why weren't THESE just
> done up separately like all the rest? Loses style points.

Moot. I never suggested that the Cappodocians be incorporated as a
bloodline of the Giovanni.

<snip>
> Second, the game balance issues become very difficult. By making
> Cappadocians have NEC, you effectively give them four disciplines;
> Mortis, Auspex, Fortitude, and Necromancy.

No. I give them three. Necromancy, if you give it 21 cards, is not
necessarily going to be any more overpowered than an other discipline with
21 cards. That 7 of these might be labelled as "Mortuus" powers is
irrelevant.

> Any Necromancy cards you
> print are not automatically restricted to the "true" Giovanni, as they
> could normally be;

Necromancy cards have never been restricted to the
"true" Giovanni. Anyone who learns Necromancy (such as the Samedi or the
Nagaraja) can practice these powers. So can the "Harbingers"/Cappodocians
who can and do practice normal Necromancy in addition to their own variant
path.

> the Cappadocians have them too,

Indeed they do. This is faithful to what White Wolf tells us about the
"Harbingers".

> so now you must
> print Giovanni-only cards instead of making them discipline-related.

No I don't. Because I never printed "Cappodocian-only" Necromancy cards
in the first place.

> Some card combinations may become an immediate issue; is there a
> reason that NEC/AUS shouldn't be combined together at such a low
> level?

Is there? Why don't you look and see? I'm pretty sure the answer is a
resounding "NO", but maybe you can find sometthing that I have missed.

> How about NEC/FOR? Is Minion Tap/Force of Will/Possession too
> powerful? Maybe not,

Probably not. Necromancy is currently the most pathetically weak of all
clan disciplines. If someone finds a good combo for it, that is good
news.

> but what else haven't you thought of?

This is what playtesting is for. Issues like this come into play
every time you print a new card.

> Players
> are creative... they'll discover things to do with old cards that the
> playtesters will overlook. Do we need more AUS/FOR vampires? How
> about the Giovanni clan toys? Ambrosius, eww... do the Cappadocians
> need Ambrosius?

They won't get him (though to me he does not seem entirely inappropriate).

> (This is one of the things that worries me about the Gargoyles people
> are mentioning; POT/PRO is one of the discipline combos that doesn't
> need to show up too easily, especially in the form POT/pro.
> POT/PRO/FOR could be even worse. Bleeds for 1 are still pretty damn
> effective, and there's always Computer Hacking once you're done
> burning all his vampires. Some disciplines DO NOT need to be
> combined, because of the existing cards.)

I do not advocate adding the Gargoyles, whom I find uninteresting. I used
them as a hypothetical example to illustrate general ideas. But there is
no reason why they could not be balanced. All the designer would have to
do is take game balance into account when designing them. There is a
simple solution to any vampire that is overpowered or undercosted: you
raise the cost, or reduce the power. If POT FOR PRO, or even just POT
FOR, is an exceptionally advantagious combination, then all you need do is
take this into account when you cost the vampire.

Such principles will not stop a stupid designer from being stupid and
costing vampires incorrectly, but there is no cure for stupidity no matter
what kind of cards you print. At this point in Jyhad's history, I think
we can be reasonably confident that we do not have a stupid designer at
the helm of the next expansion, at any rate.

> So, what happens is you end up restricting the Mortis cards too
> carefully, or worse, not carefully enough.

If he is stupid, he is sure to get it wrong. You seem to rule out the
possibility that he might be smart and get it right.

> If you had separated the
> discipline out, you wouldn't have to worry about the game balance
> issues as much,

No, because fewer people would be able to use the cards. Far fewer
possiblities. Far fewer combos to explore. Far fewer options for fun and
creative exploration. In this same spirit, perhaps you should advise
against new expansions entirely. After all, the game is fairly balanced
currently, and you never know how new cards are going to mess things
up. The fewer new card you print, the less the danger will be.

But of course, this is totally wrong. A discipline that is posessed by
more than one clan, and can be combined with more than just two other
disciplines, is hardly unprecedented, nor is it an enormous problem.

> although you'd still have to ask yourself whether or
> not the game needed more AUS/FOR vampires.

Not a problem. When you print your two 3-capacity vampires, give them
Aus-Nec or Nec-For.

> But by separating Mortis,
> you gain a significant number of benefits, some tangible, some
> intangible. Right now, there is already an AUS/FOR clan, so you can
> pretty much assume that AUS/FOR, as a combination, doesn't pose a
> significant problem to game balance.

It was a pretty safe assumption to begin with.

> This gives you great flexibility
> with creating the Mortis cards, as unless you're quite careless, you
> have difficulty "breaking" the game.

I have a better solution: design them well and don't be
careless. Then give it to the players and let them do their damndest
trying to break it.

> I tried looking at Damnans' page
> to go through his proposed Mortis cards, and it's not showing up right
> for some reason. But really, no matter what route you take with
> Mortis, whether you make it a bleed discipline, a combat discipline, a
> utility discipline, what have you, it's MUCH easier to maintain
> balance when you can separate it somewhat. Legbiter played his
> Cappadocian deck several times during his visit, and I never felt that
> it was HORRIBLY broken, even though Damnans' vampires and his cards
> are noticeably high-powered. (The Legion of Zombu, however, is just a
> no-no from the word "go".)

So you feel that if we don't let the players play with their toys much,
or allow them to play only in the approved manner, then maybe they wont
break them.

> And just because it's partly separate doesn't mean that it has to be
> TOTALLY off in its own world. The Ventrue Anti would undoubtedly be
> happy to get another few AUS/FOR vampires, to supplement themselves.
> There are several mono-FOR decks, and plenty of mono-Auspex decks that
> would be delighted to get the new low-cap vamps. Depending on what
> "fourth-discipline" skills you scattered among the clan, you could
> easily provide some support to the Toreador (include some inferior
> Presence), the Ravnos/Gangrel/Tzimisce (include some Animalism),
> Malkavians (include some Obfuscate), ... take your pick.

Necromancy has already been introduced to the game as a corner discipline
of a corner clan. Caution is all very well, but why cannot the discipline
start expanding out of its corner now? It is, after all, FAR FAR from
broken. And here's another example to introducing Mortis as Necromancy:
you can do so slowly and cautiously. You can add 3 Mortis powers in one
expansion, and 2 or 3 more in the next after you have assessed the impact
of the last three. You don't have to plonk down 10-15 new powers into the
game at one time, because it does not have to sustain itself as an entire
separate discipline.

-- John Whelan

> *That* is what matters most to us. What seems to matter most to you is
> cards not be changed, and certainly not banned.

Well, i think Andrew is making two reasonable points but perhaps not
distinguishing between them clearly enough. He is saying firstly that
Wizards have a game [namely Magic] the new expansions for which routinely
turn out to contain broken power rares which eventually have to be
banned, that this is a bad thing, and that to some extent VTES
[originally from the same stable] has the same problem. Matt's answer to
that was that Wizards ARE the market leaders in CCGs, or to put it
another way, people LIKE it that way, and don't mind a card getting
banned or fixed once they've had a chance to abuse it properly. i am sure
this strikes chords with Rob "Legacy of Pander" Treasure, and i admit to
a twinge of guilty satisfaction over the rewrite to heidelburg castle
which followed closely on the heels of its [mis]use during Legbiter's
Crusade in jyhad on-line. The seond point i think he's making is that for
new or returning players text-unsupported errata are a big turn-off
because they basically fence off a whole area of [re]discovery from the
new/returning player - a little bit like rich countries telling poor ones
that they have to go green even before they get industrial.

> As you say:
>
> > Leaving ante cards aside, this now only has three banned cards to VTES's four.
> > This makes VTES the worst CCG in this respect, worse even than Magic.
> > Shameful.
>
> I find the idea of four banned cards being "shameful" to be bizarre,
> really. I can't fathom why it bothers you so much.

Way back in the Mists of Time [just after the 7/7/98 RT rulings] we had a
right old ding-dong on the NG about banning and errata-ing problem cards.
At that time LSJ and the RT were very much in favour of errata and
against bans, so spiritually at least i think LSJ and Andrew agree about
bans - sorry if that puts unwanted words in the mouth of either
gentleman! i have the opposite view, namely that it is better to ban a
card than to issue a text-unsupported erratum. My position reflects my
belief that the tournament scene is less important for the overall health
of VTES than most people on the NG think - we need to remember that we
are unusually-committed and competitive players, and that we don't
represent the REAL jyhad-playing public, many of whom find text-
unsupported errata a real turn-off becaue it buggers up their home-made
combos.

i'd like to reinforce the point that you and Scott and Matt have made
about the experience of individual cards in play, and not Grand
Generalisations about Game Design, being the best way forward from
problem cards. In reality there is no Great Project, shameful or
otherwise, to ban cards - there are specific cards banned, for specific
reasons.

Cunctator Motion, High Stakes and Playing for Keeps are banned in
tournament play because playing for ante is an optional rule that is not
used in tournaments.

Madness of the Bard is banned because we do not have enough judges to
have one sitting in permanently on every tournament game, and even if we
did it's doubtful that they could keep up with everything that was said
by every player, and that any consensus could be reached about what
constitutes rhyme. i know the ostensible reason is to do with non-English
speakers but frankly i don't buy that one and i know at least two NES's
who find this justification faintly offensive.

Monocle of Clarity is banned because there are some truly appalling
combos around this card, based on the template: "If i do X, will you
do Y?" i sometimes wonder if these are quite as bad as people think,
given that the monocle is unique equipment, and that the combos require
an unusually-high level of cleverness to pull off. There is also a
problem about judging the MoC but it is less severe than with MotB.

Rowan Ring is banned because paralysation rules are no longer used in
VTES. A pity. i think they should be reinstated.

Return to Innocence is banned because nobody can think of a good way to
rewrite the card that both preserves its original intention [burn a big
vamp you control to bleed for loads] without shifting the game too
radically towards Stupid Big Bleed Decks. i'd suggest that if somebody
CAN think of such a fix then good for them, and us. If it happens then
maybe we can look forward to a reissue of the card with new text - for
the reasons explained above, i'd certainly NOT be in favour of it coming
back with text-unsupported errata. And in defence of the AH design team
i'd add that IMO they tried to do something worthy in that set, namely
shift the balance towards Big Vamps and Allies. That their success was
only partial is unfortunate but i think if you try anything creative you
should have the right to fail - not understanding this point is one of
the Deep Flaws in the British character, but by and large Australians,
Americans and some Europeans do get it. i think the failure of AH in
achieving these ends has laid the foundation for what i confidently
expect to be SW's success at exactly the same task [among others].

> Play balance matters to me. It's part of what attracted me to V:tES,
> (the other half being the complexity, and the montage of having that much
> complexity while still being play balanced is what makes V:tES shine.) and
> it certainly matters to me far *more* than whether 4 or 3 or 0 cards out of
> Oodles got banned.

i like play balance too, but it is not the most important thing to me.
IMO a good game is good for reasons of synergy between a number of
different factors which are different for different games. For VTES/Jyhad
these would include balance, complexity, consistency, artwork, creation
of a believable universe populated by credible personalites, social
interaction with bright people, excitement, the opportunity to express
your own creativity and personality, and lots of others probably which
i've forgotten. i think that games that go questing after balance [or
even consistency] at the expense of any other consideration can end up
losing a lot of their freshness and accessibility. IMO this happened to
Rage when it changed into Rage II and to D&D when it changed into AD&D
[arguably] and second edition [even more arguably]. And not that i play
the game, but a lot of people i know feel the same way about what
happened to SFB.
>
> All that contrariness aside, lemme say one thing in some agreement. I'm
> not sure it's clear that Rowan Ring needs to be banned, really, considering
> the amount of errata that is in existence. "Paralyze" got nixed a long time
> ago, but Wooden stake got fixed, and I can't think it's too hard to make
> text for Rowan Ring that does the intended purpose. I mean, there is the
> Amaranth/Archon combo, or just use Amaranth with Mua-cheeze, but is that
> really a "broken" combo?

i agree with you. Please, sir, can we have our paralysation back?

"Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:

> is not necessary to have a judge listening. That difficulty has been

I'm not sure what your point is. You mean, "If it's so easy to solve
the card then a judge isn't required."? I hope you don't seriously want
a response to that. Obviously, if judging the thing isn't required because
rhyming is so easy to do, then the card itself isn't required. Ban it.
No one needs to play a useless - but irritating - card.

If, on the other hand, rhyming is a potentially difficult task that some
player might actually fail at, you need to have a referee present full
time to decide when and how someone failed. If you don't, then people have
to appeal every time they think someone failed (assuming the offender does
not simply admit it - which often they probably won't). An appeal for
every blood lost? Then there's the question of, do you have to rhyme when
requesting the appeal? Or explaining it? How can you tell the judge what
wasn't a rhyme without failing to rhyme yourself? What if your recitation
of the alleged failure conflicts with offender's - who may well decide to
change it?

The problem is, this card isn't about strategy, it's about a physical task.
You can not get fair, reliable judging without the judge being physically
present to experience the incident himself - any more than you could get
reasonable scores for an olympic ice skater by having someone describe the
skater's performance to the skating judges and asking them to write down
their numbers from the description.

> >As far as the game being "what it is", what Madness of the Bard is is
> >a mistake. It's a parlor game card which got snuck into a strategy
> >game because some designer at some point in time (I'm assuming it was
> >Richard Garfield but I may be wrong) thought it was cute. If you don't
> >believe that was just a mistake, a bad move, a faux pas, whatever, the
> >vast majority of other tournament players seem to. And, as LSJ so
> >cleverly pointed out, it is less shameful to admit a mistake than to
> >ignore it.
>
> It's not a mistake - it's one of several deliberately bizarre
> Malkavian cards. That you can't stand the mechanic just demonstrates
> how effective and appropriate it is.

Hey, shooting your opponents with a real gun would also be pretty effective.
That doesn't make it "appropriate". You seem to be insinuating that if a
card is useful in advancing someone's position in the game, it is ergo
"appropriate". I'm not sure how you made that leap. Suffice it to say,
I disagree.

And it is both "deliberately bizarre" AND a parlor game - not a strategy
game - card. The latter is what makes it inappropriate.

> If you don't like it, then take a directed action to destroy
> it. Lobbying to ban the card instead is underhand.

Why? I don't like parlor games. Or at least, I don't care for them
mixed in with my strategy games. If I don't like it, and the vast majority
of the players don't like, and the current player organization doesn't
like it, who the hell are you to tell us we're stuck with it just because
you and a few of the early game designers like it? Why are cards supposed
to be stuck in the game once they get printed and can never be excised
until the end of time? How did you arrive at that rule?

Things that don't work well and don't fit in the game can be dropped. That's
not underhanded. That's fixing a problem.

Fred

Really what we found in Atlanta was that Damnan's Cappadocian concept was
pretty functional, had the right "flavour", and slotted quite well into

broken right from the word go, and saw that some are breakable quite
easily. So much might be said for any draft set of cards that are up for
playtesting.

However, i now don't think data of this kind is to the point of your
objection to more clans and disciplines. If i understand you correctly,
you are saying that even if you could get perfectly-playtested cards for

collecting it, so that most people would be unhappy with most expansions.

images. i wonder if i am alone in this perhaps rather uncritical approach
to new expansions?

colours [so why should VTES need more disciplines?] i see the disciplines
as suites of competence in particular areas. Necromancy and Mortis are
suites of competence in particular areas, and arguably they are the SAME
colour, or shades of the same colour. Other new disciplines would
correspond to multi-colour cards of which Magic has rather a lot, and
they don't seem to break that game up particularly.

>I'm not sure what your point is. You mean, "If it's so easy to solve
>the card then a judge isn't required."?

That's right.

>Obviously, if judging the thing isn't required because
>rhyming is so easy to do, then the card itself isn't required. Ban it.
>No one needs to play a useless - but irritating - card.

If the card were useless then there'd be no need to ban it. It isn't
though as, even if the rhyme is trivial, remembering to make one
isn't.

>Hey, shooting your opponents with a real gun would also be pretty effective.

SJ Games has an amusing variant of Killer called "Andrew Season".
Something to do with there being too many Andrews in gaming ...

>That doesn't make it "appropriate". You seem to be insinuating that if a
>card is useful in advancing someone's position in the game, it is ergo
>"appropriate". I'm not sure how you made that leap.

It's appropriate because it is in character for the Malkavians and
similar to their other prank cards.

>And it is both "deliberately bizarre" AND a parlor game - not a strategy

>game - card. The latter is what makes it inappropriate. Why? I don't
>like parlor games.

A serious chess player might dismiss all of VTES as a parlor game -
the luck of the draw; the table talk; the deals; the fuzzy timing; the
role-playing ambiance. But this distinction is irrelevant - the game
is defined by its rules and components, not by such stereotyping.

But, if you wish to pursue the point, take a look at Malkavian Game.
This invokes a parlor game of Rock/Scissors/Paper without even
troubling to explain the rules. You could make all the same
pettifogging objections to this:

* the finger patterns are subjective
* the game's fleeting nature and split-second timing require a keen
judging eye
* the game's rules are ill-defined.
* the game is physical and discriminates against certain classes of
folk, e.g. people with arthritis or missing fingers. I have an
unfortunate colleague who would only be able to choose Rock.

In practise, I assume players and judges are prepared to deal with
such issues by using some common sense. The same should apply to
Madness of the Bard.

>If I don't like it, and the vast majority of the players don't like,
>and the current player organization doesn't
>like it, who the hell are you to tell us we're stuck with it just because
>you and a few of the early game designers like it? Why are cards supposed
>to be stuck in the game once they get printed and can never be excised
>until the end of time? How did you arrive at that rule?

I just want to play with the cards that I've bought. It's the VEKN
who wants to stop me with their non-canonical rule - who the hell are
they? A non-rhetorical answer might be helpful. The organisation has
some formal structure I believe but what are my rights as a member?
My impression is that I have none - that this is an oligarchy not
unlike the political structure of the game's sects. In that case, you
may consider me to be an Anarch.

Andrew

get to express their opinion and have a say in the outcome?", is a good
one. The answer, in practice, is that we all express our opinions and
then LSJ and WW do what they please - and each person hopes what he pleases
is what they decide to do. (Maybe it's slightly different than that but
I think I'm in the ballpark.) I don't know that that's the only system

the notion that there is no means of changing things that were done wrong

>But, if you wish to pursue the point, take a look at Malkavian Game.
>This invokes a parlor game of Rock/Scissors/Paper without even
>troubling to explain the rules. You could make all the same
>pettifogging objections to this:

What an astonishing bunch of unmitigated CRAP you have produced here.

>* the finger patterns are subjective

Bullshit.

If two (2) fingers are extended, it is "Scissors."
If five/all fingers are extended, it is "Paper."
If no fingers are extended, it is "Rock."

There is no subjectivity about this. Those who cannot distinguish
between zero, two, and five need not be playing V:TES, sayonara, have
a nice day. Those who think that two fingers are five fingers need to
have one less pint prior to play.

>* the game's fleeting nature and split-second timing require a keen
>judging eye

Bullshit.

You count "three", and on "three", you produce a hand-sign. There are
three reasonably-disinterested other players convenient to provide
witness, even if it WERE easily possible to convert one of the above
hand-signs to another upon sight of the opponent's without anyone
noticing.

>* the game's rules are ill-defined.

Bullshit.

How is "Rock beats Scissors, Scissors beats Paper, Paper beats Rock"
ill-defined?

>* the game is physical and discriminates against certain classes of
>folk, e.g. people with arthritis or missing fingers. I have an
>unfortunate colleague who would only be able to choose Rock.

It is to be noted that such unfortunates are in the excruciatingly
slim minority, and it would be further noted that those without
fingers are not likely to be interested in a card game anyway, card
games being one of the things one pretty much *requires* fingers for,
if only to hold the bloody cards.

Such a slim minority, in fact, such a FAR SLIMMER minority than
non-native speakers (which I must assume is the parallel you are
trying to draw here), would be quite simple for a single judge to
handle during tournament play; either with physical presence for every
playing of Malkavian Game, or if he's an intelligent judge, a
determination of an easily recognizable "substitute" for Rock, Paper,
and Scissors that someone without fingers could reproduce. Perhaps
one could hold 1, 2, or 3 pool under the table in one's fingered hand.

>In practise, I assume players and judges are prepared to deal with
>such issues by using some common sense. The same should apply to
>Madness of the Bard.

Except that there is no issue above that requires any subjective
judgement, unlike Madness of the Bard.

present all the time regardless. Suppose, for example, there is a

appear? And how long do you expect it to stay in play before someone
takes it out with a directed action?

> * the finger patterns are subjective

Instead have both players take a die and turn it so that a 1, 2, or 3 is

No, it is doubly CORRECT, actually.

First, "pointless nuisance" and "useless" are two entirely different
things. Useless is just that; useless, and can be easily ignored.
Nuisances are generally classified as such because they CANNOT be
easily ignored. Ignoring this card will result in your rapid ousting.

Second, games like "Simon Says" rely on "Simon" to misdirect, confuse,
and basically trick other players into forgetting to only do what
"Simon Says"; there is no "Simon" available in V:TES. In addition,
"Simon" has an advantage in comparison to Madness of the Bard; he is
permitted to break the rules all he wants. This analogy is flawed.

Elsewhere, you claim that MotB's effect can be avoided with what must
be considered a "trivial" fudge such as ending each sentence by
stating "period." Which is it? Either MotB's requirement is not
trivial, in which case all other arguments apply, or it IS trivial, in
which case it is just a pointless nuisance and should be given the
boot from tournaments.

>>As much as you'd like to believe otherwise, a judge MUST be present
>>all the time, as nobody else can enforce disputes about whether...
>
>If players are going to be unreasonable assholes then you need a judge
>present all the time regardless. Suppose, for example, there is a

Some players are only unreasonable assholes in pressure situations.
In a late-game situation where each pool matters, some of the most
perfectly sane people have been known to flip and argue miniscule,
ridiculous things.

Nevertheless, some players WILL always be unreasonable assholes.
Since you cannot stop them from being assholes, you force a judge to
be present at all times when MotB is played, making it unworkable in
practice.

>dispute about whether a player did or did not pay a blood cost. This
>might be a matter of deliberate cheating or just a slip. In practise,
>this game currently depends upon a certain amount of player memory,
>honour and good will to function at all. More serious games like
>chess _do_ have a judge present all the time or the players record
>every move. If you want perfection then you will have to do this too.

I have played competitive chess. Recording every move takes an
insignificant amount of time; one writes something simple like "e4"
after one moves (while your opponent's time is running), and has done
with it. It takes approximately two seconds.

Recording every move and play in V:TES is also unworkable in practice.
Most things, such as paying a blood cost, are a concrete,
non-subjective occurrence. Either one did pay off the vampire, or one
didn't, and it's normally easy to go back and determine how much the
vampire originally had and whether they should have paid or not. The
onus is also somewhat on one's opponents to pay attention; but again,
with non-subjective occurrences, it's easy to point out at the time
"Hey, you didn't pay for that Blur yet."

Whether or not something someone just said rhymed is still a
subjective call, and since it is a spoken phrase with no record, it is
impossible to go back and determine. There is a difference.

>Mind you, the VEKN rules do mandate that
>
>"Officially sanctioned competition requires the physical presence of a
>head judge during play to adjudicate disputes..."
>
>So there's not really an issue here. If one judge isn't enough then

Requiring a sufficient amount of non-players who are competent to be
available; this only adds to the difficulty, since Madness of the Bard
requires full-time attention.

>deputies may be appointed. Just how often do you expect MoB to
>appear? And how long do you expect it to stay in play before someone
>takes it out with a directed action?

These statements are not relevant to the issue at hand, which is
whether or not its appearance causes several non-resolvable problems.
"It doesn't come up very much anyway" is not a good answer, sorry; not
when one knew about the problems ahead of time. And the person who
gets screwed by its appearance, or the judge who has to stand near the
table verifying every single rhyme, are not going to think it's a very
good answer either.

summon the judge, and he will arrange matters so that things can be
resolved fairly; by watching himself, if need be. He may then wander

if one player intends to play lots of them, he can be warned ahead of
time so that the judge can stay in earshot and be quickly fetched as

the common definition of the game. Perhaps a formal "definition"
could be added to the clarifications page, since it does not require
errata to Malkavian Game, and although I find the need for such a
definition slim to none, it would also not hurt anything (since it's
not errata and does not require card text changing).

>>or if he's an intelligent judge, a

It's easy to find an equivalent that still satisfies the *intent* of
Malkavian Game, you mean, which is that one should play some form of
Rock/Scissors/Paper for 2 pool.

argued to have NOT meant that players should simply repeat "period."
at the end of each of their sentences; it was obviously designed to
induce a little verbal wordplay and creativity, ie parlor game.
However, it failed. Since the INTENT of the card cannot be easily
satisfied, it is a much better solution just to ban the damn thing and
have done with it.

> James Coupe <jr...@cam.ac.uk> wrote:

> > rhyme, also known as true rhyme?
>
> Oooh...can you provide an example, James? Since my study of the
> English language focused more on linguistics/literary analysis thaan
> production/literature, I didn't get enough of a chance to see all of
> the lovely variations on rhyme you keep mentioning.

Originally found in Irish (i.e. Gaelic), hence the name, though also found
in other languages in the Celtic group. Basically, it works on the
principle that certain consonants sound similar. If you do any work on
phonetics, you tend to get certain sounds lumped together under terms like
nasals, fricatives and plosives and the like. Any vowel placed before a
vowel from one consonant group will rhyme with any other vowel placed
before a consonant from the same group.

"Deibhidhe /dev-ith-a (voiced 'th')/ or /jevy/- the most common syllabic
meter. In the dán díreach style, it is made up of rhyming couplets in
stanzas of 4 lines, or a quatrain. The rhyme is between words of unequal
syllabic length; the shorter word is called rinn /reen/, the longer one
airdrinn /ard-reen/. In Irish, rhyme begins with the first stressed vowel
of the word, and all subsequent consonants must be of the same class and
quality. There are six consonant classes: (p, t, c); (b, d, g); (ph,
th,ch); (bh, mh, dh, gh, l, n, r); (ll, mm, ng, nn, rr); (s). Any
consonant rhymes fully with itself or any other consonant in its
group. There are additional rules governing alliteration within each line
and internal rhymes."

http://www.courses.fas.harvard.edu/~laa68/handouts/IrishBardicTerms.htm

Since Madness of the Bard doesn't require you to use English rhymes, this
is a perfectly acceptable rhyme scheme to use by card text.

http://www.dnaco.net/~mobrien/irishptr/drchpoem/comharda.html

Comhardadh: how to rhyme in Irish

I hate to tell you this, but to learn how the medieval Irish rhymed their
poems, you first have to find out how they looked at the sounds of their
language. I know this looks really scary and complicated,
but bear in mind just how complicated that, say, a rap song would look,
if outlined in terms of meter and phonetics! The poet and the audience
would have had the patterns engrained in them; it's only to the outsider
or the describer that these patterns seems detailed, difficult and
strange.

In medieval Irish linguistic and poetic tracts, the sounds of Old and
Middle Irish are carefully divided into two kinds of classifications. The
first was broadness/slenderness.

Broad vowels: a, o, u, á, ó, & ú
Slender vowels: e, i, é & í
Broad consonants: Consonants immediately preceded by broad vowels
Slender consonants: Consonants immediately preceded by slender vowels.

The second classification was similar to the description of consonants
that linguists use today.
The letters in parentheses are the spellings used for the same sound when
it's not the first sound in a word.

na trí chonnsuine chruaidhe
'the 3 hard consonants' = voiced stops
b, d, g (p, t, c)
na trí chonnsuine bhoga
'the 3 soft consonants' = voiceless stops
p, t, c (pp, tt, cc)
na trí chonnsuine gharbha
'the 3 rough consonants' = voiceless spirants
ph (f), th, ch
na seacht gconnsuine éadroma
'the 6 light consonants' = voiced spirants & weak-pronounced voiced
liquids
b (v), m (nasal v), d (th as in then), g (as in morgen), l, n, r.
na cúig chonnsuine theanna
'the 5 strong consonants' = strong pronounced voiced liquids
m (mm), ll, nn, ng, rr.
Strong consonants rhyme with light ones.
connsuinne aimrid nach coír a modh ar bioth gan 's' eile na haghaidh.
(I have no idea what that means in Irish = continuants.)
S (ss).
Rhymes only with itself.

In the case of a consonant blend, the blends fell into one of the
following classes, each of which only rhymed with blends of the same
class. Following the modern scholars, '+' means before or after and '-'
means before.

Hard+Light.
Soft+Light, Soft+Rough, Light+Rough, Strong+Soft, Hard-Rough.
Rough+Light, Rough+Strong, Rough+Rough, Rough+Hard.
Light+Light, Light+Strong.
S+consonant
Rhymes when each consonant accompanying s is of the same class (Strong
& Light count as the same class for this); in Middle Irish, the
accompanying consonants are lenited for poetic purposes.

(In Middle Irish, when s is the initial sound of any part of a compound
word except the first syllable, s is lenited & soundless -- except in the
case of demonstrative suffixes or words beginning with sg, sd, sb or sm.
Also in compound words, the broadness or slenderness of the final
syllable of any component word becomes the broadness or slenderness of
the initial sound of the component following it. I don't know that you'll
ever need to know these rules, but now you do.)

Comhardadh occurs only when the first syllable of each word (the first
syllable was always stressed in Old Irish, or Middle Irish as pronounced
by poets) had the same vowel and consonants of the same class and
broadness/slenderness. The initial consonants don't count; only the
sounds in the middle and end of the syllable do. Other syllables than the
first one only need to have the same vowel if that vowel is long.

Comhardadh could be final, internal, or aicill. Aicill rhymes the final
stressed word of one line with the next-to-last unstressed word in the
next line. (In this relationship, the final rhyming word is called rinn,
'tip' and the unstressed rhyming word airdrinn, 'attention-tip'. )

Do bhíoth dhamh ag déanaimh eóil
an gheágsoin fa gar do mhaoin;
fada siar ón tírsi thuaidh
aniar uain do-chínnsi an gcraoibh.

Final rhyme: mhaoin/gcraoibh
Internal rhyme: dhamh/gar, siar/aniar, tírsi/do-chínnsi,
déanaimh/ghéagsoin
Aicill: thuaidh/uain
Pretty, isn't it? Think how appealing that kind of pattern must be to
your ear.

comhardadh slán: perfect rhyme (rhyme which follows the rules above)
comhardadh briste: imperfect rhyme (rhymes only by same vowel & same
broadness/slenderness of consonants)

A line in a couplet may include a word which rhymes with two words
instead of just one! This usually happens when the two-rhyme line has a
word which is repeated, but also in less easy ways.

In article <8v33j7$81l$1...@nnrp1.deja.com>, legb...@my-deja.com writes:

>Really what we found in Atlanta was that Damnan's Cappadocian concept was
>pretty functional, had the right "flavour", and slotted quite well into

>broken right from the word go, and saw that some are breakable quite
>easily. So much might be said for any draft set of cards that are up for
>playtesting.
>
>However, i now don't think data of this kind is to the point of your
>objection to more clans and disciplines. If i understand you correctly,
>you are saying that even if you could get perfectly-playtested cards for
>all the new clans and disciplines you would STILL be against expansions
>of this kind, because they would increase global player dissatisfaction.

More or less, though I'm still not sure you see the whole concept as I see it.
My concepts seem abstract even to me, such that I have difficulty even
articulating them as I understand them. Still, the Cappodocians provide a very
concrete example, whose lessons can be applied to almost every "new discipline"
that one might contemplate incorporating. The two approaches are 1)
incorporate Mortis as a separate discipline and give the Cappodocians
Aus-For-Mor, or 2) incorporate Mortis as a path of an old discipline, and give
the Cappodocians Aus-For-Nec. I think I have already clearly shown that option
#2 offers everything that option #1 does, but gives much more besides. It can
be clearly shown that the Aus-For-Nec approach is much more efficient, and
gives more satisfaction to a greater number of players. You not ONLY introduce
a new clan with new powers, but you ALSO keep the Giovanni happy by giving them
new toys to play with, and ALSO the new clan is more flexible because it can
use the old Necromancy powers as well as the new Mortis ones. The new powers
become more viable and full of possibilty because they can be efficiently
combined with 4 other discipines as opposed to only two. In a game which
revolves around combos, and in which powerful combos do not (or should not)
exist WITHIN a single discipline, this seems to me to be very important.

I'd rather not say that if provokes player dissatisfaction (though I suspect
this is true). I would rather say that it promotes much less player
satisfaction than the alternate, superior approach. It seems to me blatantly
obvious that a good designer does not deliberately put out a product that he
knows to be half as good as what he is capable. He does not deliberately make
second-best choices. If he does, it is his own fault if players start playing
better games whose designers are making better choices than he.

I think the ball is in your court. I have made many arguments showing why
introducing new resource-requirement categories is inferior to the alternative
approach to introducing the same powers. You need to explain why these new
Mortis power that are being introduced need to have the new skull symbol of
Mortis, as opposed to the old skull symbol of Necromancy. You need to explain
why that would make them better and more fun to play with.

>You see this happening because any new expansion would either contain
>one's favourite clan or it wouldn't, or else it would contain so few new
>cards for your favourite discipline/clan that you wouldn't bother
>collecting it, so that most people would be unhappy with most expansions.
>Is that right? i'm quite prepared to be told that i have HORRIBLY
>misunderstood you!

This is fair enough, though the statements are too absolute and removed from
the comparative context that I prefer. I would not say that the above things
are true in any absolute sense, I merely say that they are MORE true than would
be the case with the alternate, superior, non-fragmenting approach, which
introduces the same "new things" in a better way. The non-fragmenting
approach allows "cool new powers" to be more usable and accessable, and does
not try to confine them within a newly invented resource-requirement category
which makes it inaccessible to any other vampire that was previously printed.

>If it is a fair summary of your position, i would like
>to raise a tremulous talon and confess to liking ALL the vampires of ALL
>the clans except, of course, the Camarilla Toiletdoors, which means that
>i would collect ANY CONCEIVABLE expansion for the game except the
>Toiletdoors Private Party expansion. Who am i kidding, i would even
>collect that, especially if it contained lots of semi-pornographic
>images. i wonder if i am alone in this perhaps rather uncritical approach
>to new expansions?

This is all very well, but you need to consider that 1) not all players will
have your fanatic devotion, or even my fanatic devotion, and 2) would it not be
better if the expansions gave you more for your money? Would it not be better
and more efficient if, in the context of the same space requirements, the
expansion introduced a more-flexible version of the Cappodocians AND enhanced
the Giovanni, as opposed to merely the introducing a less-flexible version of
Cappodocians? Would not an expansion that was twice as good make you twice as
happy?

-- John Whelan

competitive players, and that we don't represent the REAL jyhad-playing
public, many of whom find text-
unsupported errata a real turn-off becaue it buggers up their home-made
combos.

i'd like to reinforce the point that you and Scott and Matt have made
about the experience of individual cards
in play, and not Grand
Generalisations about Game Design, being the best way forward from
problem cards. In reality there is no
Great Project, shameful or otherwise, to ban cards - there are specific
cards banned, for specific reasons.

Cunctator Motion, High Stakes and Playing for Keeps are banned in
tournament play because playing for
ante is an optional rule that is not used in tournaments.

Madness of the Bard is banned because we do not have enough judges to
have one sitting in permanently on
every tournament game, and even if we did it's doubtful that they could
keep up with everything that was
said by every player, and that any consensus could be reached about what
constitutes rhyme. i know the
ostensible reason is to do with non-English speakers but frankly i don't
buy that one and i know at least two
NES's who find this justification faintly offensive.

Monocle of Clarity is banned because there are some truly appalling
combos around this card, based on the
template: "If i do X, will you do Y?" i sometimes wonder if these are
quite as bad as people think, given that
the monocle is unique equipment, and that the combos require an
unusually-high level of cleverness to pull
off. There is also a problem about judging the MoC but it is less severe
than with MotB.

Rowan Ring is banned because paralysation rules are no longer used in
VTES. A pity. i think they should be
reinstated.

Return to Innocence is banned because nobody can think of a good way to
rewrite the card that both
preserves its original intention [burn a big vamp you control to bleed
for loads] without shifting the game
too radically towards Stupid Big Bleed Decks. i'd suggest that if
somebody CAN think of such a fix then good
for them, and us. If it happens then maybe we can look forward to a
reissue of the card with new text - for
the reasons explained above, i'd certainly NOT be in favour of it coming
back with text-unsupported errata.
And in defence of the AH design team i'd add that IMO they tried to do
something worthy in that set, namely
shift the balance towards Big Vamps and Allies. That their success was
only partial is unfortunate but i
think if you try anything creative you should have the right to fail -
not understanding this point is one of
the Deep Flaws in the British character, but by and large Australians,
Americans and some Europeans do
get it. i think the failure of AH in achieving these ends has laid the
foundation for what i confidently expect
to be SW's success at exactly the same task [among others].

> Play balance matters to me. It's part of what attracted me to
V:tES,
> (the other half being the complexity, and the montage of having that
much
> complexity while still being play balanced is what makes V:tES shine.)
and
> it certainly matters to me far *more* than whether 4 or 3 or 0 cards
out of
> Oodles got banned.

i like play balance too, but it is not the most important thing to me.
IMO a good game is good for reasons of
synergy between a number of different factors which are different for
different games. For VTES/Jyhad
these would include balance, complexity, consistency, artwork, creation
of a believable universe populated
by credible personalites, social interaction with bright people,
excitement, the opportunity to express
your own creativity and personality, and lots of others probably which
i've forgotten. i think that games
that go questing after balance [or even consistency] at the expense of
any other consideration can end up
losing a lot of their freshness and accessibility. IMO this happened to
Rage when it changed into Rage II and
to D&D when it changed into AD&D [arguably] and second edition [even
more arguably]. And not that i play
the game, but a lot of people i know feel the same way about what
happened to SFB.
>
> All that contrariness aside, lemme say one thing in some agreement.
I'm
> not sure it's clear that Rowan Ring needs to be banned, really,
considering
> the amount of errata that is in existence. "Paralyze" got nixed a
long time
> ago, but Wooden stake got fixed, and I can't think it's too hard to
make
> text for Rowan Ring that does the intended purpose. I mean, there is
the
> Amaranth/Archon combo, or just use Amaranth with Mua-cheeze, but is
that
> really a "broken" combo?

i agree with you. Please, sir, can we have our paralysation back?

" ENDQUOTE

In the recent changes to the RPG, Mortis is now a subset 'Path' of
Necromancy... more or less... much like Walk of Flames is a Path of
Thaumaturgy. So including Mortis powers as a set of cards compatible with
Necromancy would be consistent in both game terms and World of Darkness
terms... It is possible for Giovanni vampires to learn Mortis and it is
possible for say Harbingers to learn the Sepulchre Path...

my opinion as they are they don't compete at all. Of all the 'independents',
the Giovanni are probably the least able to compete. Some of the existing
Necromancy cards are completely useless... I mean, 'Eyes of the Dead' ? Come
on... that card bites. What we need are BETTER Necromancy cards... not a
slight variation of Necromancy that can't be played by Giovanni.

Cheers,

The DCI banned all of the cards that are currently on the V:EKN
banned list. Madness of the Bard and Return to Innocence were the
last to be added to the list, and were added after the point in
time in which I became the rules authority - not that there's
necessarily any connection - just food for your theories.

which eventually became 6 and then went back to 2 briefly) before
the DCI eventually adopted their version of the SPTR - the DCI's

Does "the anal folk who play CCG" include yourself or not? Since you

"*their* precious cards", I am left assuming that you refer to players other

> Myself, I always thought that ante was a clever idea of Garfield's but
> found that, in practise, the clash with my own collecting instinct

"Pangs?" Are you for real?
"It's a shame that we can't live up to his expectations?" Once again,
the "Founding Fathers" of V:tES are beyond reproach, and it's only the
inability of "us shameful, anal players" to see the True Wisdom of the
original designers.
For as much as you seem able to construct coherent sentences, Andrew,
you really can belt out some absolute nonsense. I'd be pleased to hear that
you're just pulling our collective leg, and don't believe this one bit, and
I'd be the first to admit I was trolled into it, because I can't reconcile
it any other way.

On the topic, though, I would never want to play with ante because it
would mean that I would *have* to make a deck that I thought would never get
ousted if I wanted to use any cards I didn't have many of. The point of
winning V:tES, however, is to earn VPs, only one of which you can earn by
being the last man standing. If I win 3/5 VPs at a table for 3 ousts and am
then ousted, I have won the game, but lost my ante. As VPs are intangible,
but cards are tangible, I risk something for nothing. Yes, yes, I've picked
up 3 ante cards, but we're back "cards I didn't have many of". They can all
play Gangrel Untap Walls with all common cards, but I can't make a Giovanni
deck and use my one copy of Ambrosius, since the risk is too great. This
limits my deck choices to common cards, even if I'm making a deck that can
win a table with 3/5 VPs.
Ante was introduced in Magic, a primarily 2 player game, where winner
takes all. A deck is desiged to:
Win
or
Win.
This mechanic does not carry over to V:tES, with the Predator/Prey
relationship and where the games are almost always 4-6 people. I begin to
support James Coupe's theory that you haven't played this game anywhere near
as much as the rest of us, if you've even ever played at all.

On top of all that, I'm playing with my playgroup to have fun, not to

Well, now that they've fixed Life Boon, yes, that's always true. =)
But what I meant was you only get *a* VP for being last man standing. You
got the other one for ousting your prey, as always.
I guess you could have a very "passive oust," like them transferring
themselves out, or two guys wiping each other out in a vote or something,
but in general, you got one VP for being there, but you had to DO something
for the other one. If you had a deck that JUST lived, and did *no* damage
to it's prey (a BloodDoll/Regenerating/ReformBody deck or something silly
like that) you can't get a VP, just 1/2 for timing out.
For most games, of course, you're completely right. The 2 VP "Wall"
deck is certainly a strategy people have tried.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 27 Nov 2000 04:27:40 -0500, Pat Ricochet wrote:

>On the topic, though, I would never want to play with ante because it
>would mean that I would *have* to make a deck that I thought would never get
>ousted if I wanted to use any cards I didn't have many of.

That's the point of ante. It's a balancing mechanism which is
designed to discourage the use of rare cards. It is _meant_ to be a
factor that you take into account when you build your deck.

I wonder if Cantila and his Swedish chums have tried using ante
instead of a CL? It's perfect for the situation where you have a
limited card supply in a closed circle of players. If one player uses
"too many" of a particular card then, over time, the effect of ante
will be to redistribute the wealth. The more of a card that they use,
the more likely it is to become the ante.

Andrew
